Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
So as we were driving back from the New York Qualifier last night,
during the post game analysis of my pal Ben's crashing and burning with
what should be (and tends to be locally) a very solid IC member/Orlando
vote deck for the second tournament in a row, it turned out that in both
this qualifier and the Origins Qualifier, Ben got completely killed in
two (of 6 total) games by randomly getting his Lutz contested. I pointed
out that I can't remember the last time that I actually had a vampire
contested or was in a situation where it was actually problematic that a
vampire I had in my uncontrolled region was already in play under
someone else's control (as opposed to it just being mildly annoying),
and that losing games due to contestation is just incredibly random
punishment. Yeah, Lutz is really good and really popular, so he is more
likely to be contested than, like, Gabriel de Cambrai or something, but
still, having a big important vampire getting contested is both
incredibly random and usually completely game destroying from very early
in the game.

As vampire contestation (specifically big vampire contestation--when Old
Netdecker is contested, it is hardly a problem. When the IC member your
deck is relying on to go, or whatever, is contested, your game is
generally over before it even starts) is soooo incredibly random (how
many vampires are in the game now?), it seems like it might be prudent
to make it less completely devastating when it happens. What we came up
with was that maybe the game would work better for all involved if when
a vampire was contested, instead of both players losing control of that
vampire, you got to alternate control of him instead. Something like:

"If two (or more) copies of a unique minion are in play, both are
flipped over and considered out of play. During each player's untap
phase, they must pay a pool to flip over their copy of the minion into
play (and flip over their opponent's copy out of play) and may use the
vampire as normal until their opponent does the same on their untap
phase. They may choose to not pay a pool and burn their copy of the
minion immediately."

I'm sure it could be worded better, buy in any case, the end result
would be that you still burn a pool each turn like normal, but instead
of just not having a vampire, you get that guy on your turn and until
your opponent's turn. There certainly could be disparity in terms of how
long each player has the minion in play, i.e. if me and my prey are
contesting a guy, I only get the guy on my turn, and then get the guy
during their turn, and then all the way around the table till my turn
again, but I suspect that the advantage that was gained by being the
predator in that situation (i.e. I get my guy to attack my prey and he
doesn't have that guy to defend himself) would balance that out.

I don't think this would be necessary for unique non minion cards--you
don't generally lose the game on T4 when someone contests your Ivory Bow
or KRCG News Radio or anything, where you do often lose the game
starting on T4 when someone contests (or brings out the big important
guy you have 10 pool on in your uncontrolled region), but a rules tweak
like this would really help mitigate the incredibly crippling and
incredibly random loss that is dropped on you just 'cause of the
incredibly small chance of someone contesting your important guy.

Peter D Bakija
pd...@lightlink.com
http://www.lightlink.com/pdb6/vtes.html

On a more serious response,
I am one of those people who thinks that contestation of vampires is rare
enough that you just have to deal with those "sucks to be you" games; it
isn't much worse than having some other bad matchup.
And in a tournament, "there's always next round".

BUT...

If I were to design a change to the contestation rules, it would be to
allow you to resolve the contest by paying pool back-and-forth all at
once, during the first untap phase of one of the contesters.

That is:
Player A brings out Lutz.
Player B brings out Lutz. They become contested.
On Player A's turn, player A may choose to burn a pool, then player B
may choose to burn a pool, then A, then B, etc, until one of the players
is ousted or yields.

Something like that?

It's not remotely how it works in practice - getting to the end much
more quickly removes most of the effects of contesting minion cards.
This method is interesting to think about for how it would completely
change how contestation works.

The only reason to contest with this system is if you know you will
win or do so much damage to the other player that it sets you up for
VPs (or spite the other player massively if you aren't trying to get
VPs).

Under the current system, there are all kinds of temporary contests
possible when people are playing the same unique minions, most of
which are horrible for one or both players. But, having one of the
players get ousted will end the contest, which can completely change
the board position.

This system is far cleaner, but I don't know that it helps the
screwjob that is contesting any.

Rather than chime in elsewhere in the thread, on the subject of its
randomness. True, choosing to contest isn't random. Being in a
position to contest is incredibly random, even here where we see
contestations or discussions to avoid contestations often enough that
it's a meaningful problem.

Not long ago, my grandpredator decided not to contest my ... Fakir.
That still screwed me as my predator had no predator all game. I've
contested Samedi in the past several years. I contested Ezmerelda to
lock up a game.

Even with the vast number of crypt options and a wide open metagame,
similar lines of thinking do result, which is fine when they happen at
different times and not so much when they happen at the same time.
Forget Lutz, in our environment, I'd be worried about contesting
Lucian, The Perfect right now.

And yet, this is a consequence of playing 'popular' crypts in
tournaments.

The same dilemma has been facing folks in the last several years when
they wanted to play Arika-centric decks (or even Law Firm in general)
- there's been a decidedly non-zero chance of seeing somebody else
playing the same general crypt in a tournament.

Same holds true for 1/2 big cap Lasombra vote decks - you won't always
run into them, but there's a reasonably small chance of it occuring.

(I've seen contestation issues for both of the above crypts in
tournaments this year, even.)

Lutz happens to be fairly popular at the moment. This isn't hard to
fathom by reading tournament reports and talking to other players
about what they see in their own tournaments. Heck, I think I have
seen at least one Lutz deck in _every_ tournament I have played in
this year save the smallest, and in several of those there were
multiple Lutz decks.

If you build a deck around huge vampires and focus on a very popular
vampire (or set of popular, large vampires), you run the risk of
contesting.

This is a metagame choice on your part - your friend could have
decided it was worth the trouble to include a Praxis: Solomon, or to
negotiate with people ahead of time. Or he could have thought "boy, I
might be contesting with folks, maybe I should play something else
instead."

> Rules aren't "random".  And it only comes up when the next player

What is random is being in the position to be contesting a vampire in
the first place. Which is completely and utterly random. It was much
less random when the rule was first invented--when there were only,
like, 110 total vampires, contestation was a significant issue to
worry about and much less of a "I happened to get hit by a meteor"
hosing. Now, with 1300+ vampires, it is incredibly unlikely to sit
down at a table with someone who has the same minion as you. And then
have them draw that minion. And then have them play that minion.
*That* is what is random. And as often, the consequences are so hugely
game destroying, it makes sense to me to at least attempt to minimize
the game destroying impact of such a random event.

And again, going back to the original example--player A puts 10 pool
on an 11 cap vampire. His prey brings out the same 11 cap vampire,
because he is one transfer ahead. Player A's game is pretty much over
at this point, even *without* actually contesting the vampire. He has
already spent 3 turns not getting out a vampire, and is going to spend
another 3 turns (given a big vampire deck) getting out his first
vampire (that is *6* turns and, say, 20 pool invested before a single
minion hits the table. What deck in what circumstance is still going
to be standing after this?). And then it is going to take 5 more turns
to recoup the 10 pool invested in the first vampire. And there is
still only 1 minion in play. This is a completely random "my game is
over" due to the contestation rules. Even without anyone choosing to
contest a minion.

-Peter

Still pretty harsh. Somebody loses X (the capacity of the vampire, not to
mention the transfers involved and the cost in pool, blood, and card play of any
cards or other effects on the the yielded vampire) and somebody else loses Y
(the winning bid amount).

Sometimes a lesser evil to standard contesting. But sometimes more.

If the rule is to be changed, better to dive headlong:

Off the top of my head:

Contesting crypt cards is handled via something akin to Banishment: when another
copy of a unique crypt card enters play, all copies are returned to the
uncontrolled region (all temporary control effects are broken).

(A good reason to keep blood on your star vampire).

Trivia for the smattering of effects that care about contested vampires:
The vampires are considered contested until one returns to play (ending the
contest, although the other copies are not actually yielded). The "cost to
contest" is zero (which may be increased by Democritus). Being made to yield a
contested card (via Democritus or Praxis Solomon) still results in that
contested card being sent to the ash heap, as normal. Olugbenga's special is
pretty useless except when Democritus is also around.

Contesting titles is as normal.
Contesting library cards is as normal.

Just an idea. If any idea is needed (and I don't say that any is).

> contestation rules are providing that offsets the bad thing that Peter
> is describing?  Would deck diversity really change noticeably if we
> got rid of vampire contestation (between players) altogether?>

How about making contestation of unique vampires work this way:

- Pay 1 pool in your untap to maintain the contest (or don't and
yield, burning as usual).

- The contested vampire can't interact with itself: Can't block or
react if the other copy is acting, can't enter combat with the other
copy, conduct your own sub-referendum if it wants to vote (usually
tied, but modifiers can change that).

Both players get to use their copy of the vampire, both get the
vampire for the same period of play, both are suffering the drag of
trying to contest their influence. The vampire takes on different
statistics while serving with each Methuselah (different blood totals,
different equipment, etc.).

Not quite as simple as Peter's plan, but does allow you to have the
vampire all the time.

Alex

Peter,
What I'm trying to say is that reshaping the "Contesting Rule"
reshapes the game in a number of other ways you potentially aren't
thinking of.

Fame is one of the key ousting mechanics for Combat Decks. A number
of decks who can't protect themselves reliably from a Combat Deck may
consider including a Fame JUST to contest it. Both the offensive Fame
and the "counter" Fame are neutered by this change to the rule. And
what happens when the Fames keep bouncing in and out?

I think it actually becomes a whole lot less predictable. It punishes
other tactics in strange ways (my wall with the Ivory Bow & Bowl of
Convergence only exists in my turn so it is valid to untap them before
paying the contest? After the contest? Can you untap a vampire that is
not controlled because of contesting?)

Seriously, messing around with this rule is likely to force a whole
raft of secondary rule changes, changes to long standing rulings and
more. Sure it is suck-tastic if you contest your Superstar Cross-
table, but as people have pointed out... it is avoidable and those who
do contest vampires cross table deliberately are either a) trying to
screw you for later, b) jackassing around, c) have built a deck that
is so narrow that even they cannot see it working in another way.

Contesting and being burned are what has always been (and possibly
always should be) the glass jaw of the Superstar Decks.

As noted, I don't think my suggested rule (or LSJ's) discourage deck
diversity. Contestation (or whatever it is in the case of LSJ's "you
just become uncontrolled" idea) still blows. It still costs you pool.
And still punishes you for having the same guys as someone else. So it
is still worth trying to avoid duplicating vampires.

That being said, I don't think it is contestation that encourages deck
diversity. Even if you are playing the most obvious net-deck in the
world, the likelihood of sitting at a table with someone who has the
same vampires as you *and* them drawing them all and wanting to play
them all is so small as to not be worth worrying about (which isn't
justification for not wanting the rules changed, but is justification
for not thinking it makes people diversify their decks). Heck. At the
finals to the Origins Qualifier, Dave Litwin and I were playing
essentially the exact same deck (G1/2 Nosferatu Breed/Boon, of which,
by the way, I have one of the first ones of in the TWDA :-), and the
only vampire we had in common in our opening crypt draws was Agripina.
I mean, we could have both drawn the exact same guys, at which point
both of our games would have been over, but by pure chance, he got
Selma and Nik and I got Murat and Calebros, so we got to play the
game.

The game itself encourages diveristy. Yeah, contestation can kill you
if you accidentally have the exact same guys as someone else at the
table, but I think the risk of contestation is low enough in most
cases that the gain of playing an obvious netdeck (i.e. a proven, good
deck) vastly outweighs the chance of outright loss due to minion
overlap.

Which doesn't make the outright loss due to minion overlap any more
palatable when it happens. It's just that I don't think the current
contestation rules actually encourage deck diversity any more than a
tweaked contestation rule (such as the one LSJ or I proposed) would.

-Peter

The contestation rules (among other things) provide a powerful check
against potentially overpowered cards (minion and not). When a card is
unique, there is a mechanism by which any other player at the table
could (in principle) remove that card from play, as well as increasing
the effective cost of that card through the contestation mechanism
itself.

In effect, were any unique card truly broken, it's effect on the
metagame would be naturally diminished by the simple fact that many
people would play it (either specifically to use it or specifically to
contest it). That doesn't mean the card isn't broken - Succubus Club
eventually got banned, for example. But even before the rules team
decided to actually ban the card, you had a defense mechanism you
could use: contestation. The game itself ends up surviving a
relatively long deliberation process before actually banning the card.

Many of the suggestions in this thread would provide similar checks,
though necessarily less strong, since the entire point of any of them
is to make contestation of large (and therefore presumably powerful)
vampires less painful.

I'd definitely include contestation in the rules were I creating the
game anew. Maybe not the exact ones we have, but something similar.

-witness1

It's been pretty clear for a while now that Kevin's responding to
arguments nobody is actually making, and seems to be carrying on a
conversation with a strawman that nobody is actually espousing.

To be clear: Kevin, I haven't seen anyone arguing that it's the actual
contestation of a vampire that's problematic or random. As you say,
that's completely a choice, and I don't think anyone is trying to
claim it isn't. What's random is this:

You have 4 minions in your uncontrolled region. You start
transferring to the strategically-best one of them. You have no idea
what anyone else is playing, and they don't know what you're playing.
You're, say, 7 pool into a 10 cap. Or whatever. Some large
investment, good strategic sense, etc. And cross-table or something,
suddenly, that 10-cap another player brings up randomly turns out to
be the same vampire.

Now, you're screwed by the contestation mechanics even if you don't go
ahead contesting. You're out a lot of transfers, have a big pool
investment you don't have time to get back, and still have no vampire,
whether you choose to contest the vamp or not. Because of random
chance - not because it's your star vamp, not because it's crucial for
your deck to function, not because it's some incredibly common
vampire, not because you made an informed choice, but just because,
randomly, out of 1300 vampires, the same one showed up and got brought
out before you - you've been short-changed to an extent that, most
likely, your game isn't playable. Remember, we're talking first
minions here, and we're talking about having the choice between being
screwed alone, or also dragging down your crosstable buddy.

Do you disagree that that's random?
Do you disagree that that's devastating to a game?
Do you disagree that the outcome is due to the contestation mechanics
currently in place, even if the mechanics aren't actually used because
the vampire isn't contested?

Because those three points are the core of the discussion the rest of
this thread has been trying to have while you've been vociferously
saying that contesting is a choice.

- D.J.

This is true even for vampires. I recently played a game in which my
predator did not bring out Anson because I had brought out Anson
first. According to him, it killed his game. Anson is a very
powerful card, and his uniqueness creates a limit to his power.

I absolutely think that unique copies of vampires should not be in
play at the same time. LSJ's idea for "banishing" crypt cards if
another copy is brought into play seems reasonable. It fits with the
concept of the game: two Methusalehs vie for control of a vampire,
each using his own methods and resources. Why should the vampire be
entirely out of play during this? A vampire is an active agent.
Sometimes it will act for one Methusaleh, sometimes for another,
depending on which most recently has sufficiently influenced it.

The main balance question with this technique is that a vampire whose
abilities are useful during others' turns will be more valuable during
a contestation than those whose abilities are useful during a
Methusaleh's own turn. For instance, Anson's special ability might
not be used by anyone if control of him keeps going back and forth
during Methusalehs' influence phases. However, the abilities of Arika
or Leandro would still be relevant.

As for the contestation of other cards, I cannot rationalize why a
unique piece of equipment played on a minion could be contested,
period. There is only one Ivory Bow. Helena has it in her
possession. Black Cat equips it and then neither can use it, but
their respective Methusalehs struggle over its possession?? How can a
vampire take an action to equip an item in the possession of someone
else? I think the contestation rules for other unique cards, such as
locations makes sense, since two Methusalehs may be warring over the
same turf, leaving it useless for both of them.

However, it would probably add an unnecessary layer of complexity to
the game to create different contestation rules for different types of
cards.

Okay, I admit there's some strawman-ness in this point, but assume
there was a rule in the rulebook that said, "at the beginning of a
game, roll percentile dice. On a roll of 00: you lose, remove your
cards from the table and try to find something else to do for the next
2 hours while other people play the game." That rule adds nothing to
the game, it simply adds a random, remote possibility that you lose
for no good reason. It would obviously be a bad rule.

Obviously, contestation isn't the same as that hypothetical "You're
Boned" rule. It's in the game for a reason and definitely adds
*something*. But the original point is that contesting is similar to
the You're Boned rule, in that what it adds to the game is not enough
to offset the possibility that you're randomly hosed and can't do
anything about it. You may not agree that that's true (and I think
there's certainly some question about whether it's bad enough to
suggest a rules change - I think the original post is more
hypothetical than anything... not necessarily "I think that this
should be changed," but more "What if this got changed - would that be
good? And if so, *should* it be changed?"), but there's definitely
something there to consider...

On Jul 14, 2:39 pm, librarian <aucti...@superfuncards.com> wrote:
> Sometimes you get screwed in seating not related to contesting.  Should
> we change the rules to prevent that too?

No. That kind of screwage is the result of two people choosing to make
decks, each with strengths and weaknesses which are deliberately
designed into their decks. If you see a weakness in your deck and
choose to ignore it, and later get hosed by that decision, it's the
result of intentionality on your part.

Vampire contestation screwage isn't something you can reasonably build
for or against. It strips player intentionality out of the game, which
is a Bad Thing design-wise.

> The other thing about this discussion that is sort of bothering me is
> that you have said repeatedly that it happens *rarely*.  If so, why
> bother with a rules change?

Why keep a rule that adds nothing good to the game and only makes
people unable to play, even if that rule effects the game only rarely?
Fred Scott mentioned inertia as a reason to avoid change, which is
probably as good a reason as any to not make any actual changes in the
game, but we're just shooting the hypothetical shit here, and don't
need to worry about such constraints.

(As a pre-emptive response to people complaining about my use of "adds
nothing good to the game" above: Due to what folks have written in
this thread, at this point I'm willing to concede that vampire
contestation can offer interesting randomness and potential stopgap
fixes to design errors, but just as often or moreso it introduces
random, uninteresting screwage.)

John Eno

As noted, the point is to make the incredibly random utter deck

Sure. But "I might contest all my weenie dementation vampires" is
likely the last thing that factors in. I won't play a superstar deck
in competition, because:

A) I might not draw the superstar.
B) The superstar might get killed.
C) Pentex Subversion is incredibly common.
D) The superstar might get contested.

So in that instance, yeah, contestation is an issue, but the last one.
But as superstar decks tend to fall under the "diverse and
entertaining" pool of decks, here is a situation where the rules for
contestation *decrease* deck diversity. I'd far sooner play a weenie
dementation deck in competition than I would a superstar deck. As I'm
concerned about contesting when playing a ridiculous superstar deck.
I'm not for a second concerned about contesting with a weenie
dementation deck (or whatever obvious netdeck you'd care to use as an
example).

> Firstly: If your prey "randomly" pulls out vampires, you should be
> able to win quite easily.

Holy crap. Why are you all so hung up on the use of the word "random"
in this discussion?

There are 1300+ vampires in the game. Whether or not anyone at a given
table has the same vampires as you in their crypt in a given game is
exactly that--random. Completely and utterly random. Pure chance.

Are some individual vampires more likely to show up in any individual
game? Sure. I'd expect to see, say, Anson or Arika more often, in the
grand scheme than I would, say, Apolonius. But that doesn't mean that
when you are playing a deck based on Anson, and you sit down at a
tournament game and someone else is also playing an Anson deck, it is
any less of a random event. So even if you arbitrarily assign odds to
each vampire of showing up, if Anson shows up 4 times more often than
Apolonius, Anson showing up in a given game is *still* random.

plays Angus the Unruled in every deck he ever plays, and you sit down
for a game with Phil and are playing your very own Angus the Unruled
superstar deck, not so random. Otherwise? Random.)

-Peter

something that would be easy to fix.

There is one element to this entire debate, one that Kevin hits on
repeatedly, Chris Berger is talking about and a few others...

Messages.Author: Fizeront
Messages.Body:
Interesting thread, so I'm giving my opinion.
First, I DO see a lot of contesting in tournaments, and Lutz is just
one of the many I see contested, Theo, Arika, Beast, are just another
examples, but I don't think that the contesting rule is the problem,
but the lack of a fast way to react to the fact that the vampire
you've been investing on would now be useless and contested if put
into play.
So I don't think it's the rule of contesting the one that needs to be
changed (and certainly not in the "We're contesting but we're not,
because we both pay but we both can use the vampire also" way that
Peter defends), but adding something like:

- Any player may spend 4 transfers and show all players a unique crypt
card from her uncontrolled zone that is controlled by another player
to move all counters on that card to another crypt card in her
uncontrolled zone.

to the Influence phase rules.
That way, in the example given, the would be screwed player just shows
everybody that Lutz, spends 4 transfers, and moves the 10 blood
counters her Lutz has to another of her uncontrolled vampires (ideally
a ten cap) to resume playing. That way she's punished from playing
that popular vampire without the desire to have it contested, but she
can continue playing.

Not really. It's when those two (or one of them) can't make some deal
or handle a game without their fav vamp.
And that comes more from not thinking about the contesting rule when
building a deck than from the complete randomness in outer space.

> > If I have Lutz in my uncontrolled and someone else has him in game,
> > it's not a die in my head that determines whether I influence him out
> > or not.
>
> And if you had 10 pool on Lutz when someone else gets Lutz out, either
> you are completely screwed, or you bring him out and contest him, and
> you are both completely screwed.
>
> Actively contesting a minion is not random. Being in a situation where
> contestation is even a possibility is completely random.

No, it's not. For someone who doesn't think about contesting when
creating or picking decks it might seem that way, I suppose. When
going to a tournament, I try to foresee what decks I'm most likely to
encounter. Arika and Anson (well, all the three A's) are vampires that
comes to mind as more risky to play due to the risk of contesting (in
a semi large, general tournament, that is).
The contest rule makes the strongest vampires slightly weaker, since
more people might want to play them. Unless you don't care about the
rule until you end up in the position where you're faced with the
choice of contesting or not. Then the rule mostly screws you over. But
that's a position where you placed yourself, in that case. At least
partially.

Being in a situation where a player smooth talks the table into giving
him undeserved victory points isn't really random either. Or a
situation where you get cross table rushed. Or a situation where you
get screwed by the wrong kind of deck being your predator/prey. Or a
situation where a table goes to time 3 minutes before you can seal the
gw.
Getting seated at the table where the smooth talker is, instead of the
table with the newbie. That's completly random. Trying to deal with
the 3-4 players you get seated with is a part of the game. If you're
trying to get them to not throw KRC points into you, not rush your
vampires or not contest with you is all the same.

> > That's random, yes. As random as if that person would've influenced
> > out Mattias when you have spend 8 pool and transfers at Nakthoreb.
> > Neither of those situations leads to an inevitable contest though. The
> > contest is a choice.
>
> Holy crap. Whether or not the contestation actually occurs is
> irrelevant. If I have 8 pool on a vampire, and someone across the
> table brings out the exact same vampire first, by pure random chance,
> I'm screwed. Even if I don't choose to contest that vampire.

It's not irrelevant. If you have a choice whether to start contesting
Lutz or not, you have a situation where you have leverage against the
player with Lutz on the table.
And again, if you're screwed beyond the possibility of getting a
single vp by that fact then there's more to it than just those 8 pool
(like an aggressive predator, a lazy ass grand predator, poorly built
deck etc.).

To me it looks more like the problem is on your side. You keep saying
that it's random, that one's screwed if someone uses the same vampires
as oneself and that you don't consider contesting when building/
picking decks.
Playing by the (current) rules and taking them into consideration when
building decks might be better than creating a whine thread here. I've
contested minions and won games. I've seen others do that too. If your
deck is built to handle one (or more) of your minions disappearing,
you have a chance (even if it's much smaller, ofc) to get a vp or two
anyway.

In the end though, the reality is that sometimes you win and sometimes
you don't. If a loss is due to contesting, timing, predator playing
the "wrong" deck, grand predator sucking or something else doesn't
matter much. All those things are a part of the game, and they
contribute to it (even if I get screwed by, and temporary dislike some
of them).

presented a jackpot-winning ticket, you could choose not to present yours.
P: But being in that situation is random
Z: But that's not what you said

with greater risk. And some jackpots are more widely played for (i.e., the
bigger the jackpot, the more tickets sold). One should acknowledge that and use
that information.
L: But after choosing to play and selecting your numbers and matching the
jackpot numbers, it's still random to have to split it with someone else.

I think one should acknowledge that there is a random element involved in
winding up at a table in which contesting (or having a choice to contest) comes
up at all.

Making a deal is completely irrelevant when you spend the first 6
turns of the game without a vampire in play. Or spending three of the
6 contesting a vampire without another minion in play, as you bring
someone else out. If you start the game with the first minion you are
bringing out already hitting the table before you bring yours out,
deal making is irrelevant. You will be ousted before you have a minion
in play.

> And that comes more from not thinking about the contesting rule when
> building a deck than from the complete randomness in outer space.

No, no it does not. Whether or not someone else at the table is
playing and influencing out the same minion as you is completely
random.

> No, it's not.

Do you understand what "random" means? There are 1300+ minions in the
game. If I have minion X in my crypt, and then I shuffle and
(randomly) draw minion X into my opening crypt draw, for contestation
to even be a *possibility*, the following things need to happen:

A) Someone in the room has to have selected minion X out of the 1300+
minions in the game and put them in their crypt.

B) They need to have ended up at the same table as me.

C) They needed to have shuffled and also (randomly) drawn minion X
into their opening crypt draw.

D) They needed to decide to start influencing out that vampire.

This is a chain of events that is governed primarily by random chance.
Yes. Some vampires are more likely to show up than others. But even
then, the odds of a given specific vampire showing up in someone's
deck, at the same table, in their opening crypt draw, and then be
influenced before anyone has any information about what minions are in
play, is very, very small. And random.

Yes. Once and a while, all these things line up, and then someone will
specifically contest a minion for strategic reasons. That isn't what
I'm talking about.

> For someone who doesn't think about contesting when
> creating or picking decks it might seem that way, I suppose.

Even if you put all the thought in the world into whether or not a
minion might be contested, being put in a situation where contestation
is a possibility is still a completely random event. I could have gone
to the last tournament and said "Huh. I want to be sure I don't even
contest a primary minion. To that end, I'm going to make a deck that
revolves around one of the worst vampires I can think of. Lucretia the
Cess Queen. No one will ever contest her!" and yet someone at that
tournament was playing a Lucretia, Cess Queen superstar deck. If we
sat at the same table, we would both be completely screwed. By utter,
random chance.

> When
> going to a tournament, I try to foresee what decks I'm most likely to
> encounter.

And yet whether or not you encounter them is a completely random
event. Or sit next to them. Or have the same minions as someone in
their opening crypt draw.

Yes. You can mitigate the likelihood of contestation by trying to read
the metagame. But still, being put into a situation where contestation
is a possibility is pure randomosity. If you say "I will avoid playing
Arika, as she is likely to be contested!", and go to a tournament
where everyone else came to the exact same conclusion, no one will
ever contest Arika (which is a random event), but the likelihood of
contesting other vampires has increased (randomly) by virtue of Arika
being removed from the pool of total minions.

You might like to think that by being super clever and trying to read
the metagame to avoid contesting minions makes being in a situation
where contestation is a possibility less random. It doesn't. You can
build the most contestation resistant deck in the world (well, ya
know, other than making it all out of Aabt Kindred) and still end up
randomly in a situation where contestation is a problem for you.
'Cause being in a situation where contestation is a possibility is
random.

> It's not irrelevant. If you have a choice whether to start contesting
> Lutz or not, you have a situation where you have leverage against the
> player with Lutz on the table.

How are you missing (or actively ignoring) the point that *you don't
even need to be actively contesting a minion to still be screwed*. The
choice is irrelevant in many situations. I am influencing out big
vampire X. I invest multiple turns and multiple transfers getting out
vampire X. Right before I get out vampire X, my prey brings out
vampire X (by pure random chance). I have a significant amount of
pool, transfers, and time invested in that minion. I now can:

A) Bring him out and contest him and screw us both.

or

B) Start bringing out a new minion, who might be just as big, and take
just as long, and be without any minions at all for a really long
time, and have a bunch of pool invested in a minion that will never
see play, and I'll probably be ousted before I see that investment
returned.

Does actually contesting the minion come into play here? No, unless I
feel spiteful, and I want to screw both of us extra hard. But the
*rules* of contestation have essentially ended my game before it even
started. By pure random chance.

> And again, if you're screwed beyond the possibility of getting a
> single vp by that fact then there's more to it than just those 8 pool
> (like an aggressive predator, a lazy ass grand predator, poorly built
> deck etc.).

Please read the above example. Now read it again. And don't ignore it.
Go on. I'll wait.

Really. Go reread it. As I have presented it multiple times now, and
you still don't seem to see what I am talking about.

In the situation as presented, which isn't that far out of the realm
of reason (you can say all you want "Well, if your opening crypt is
all big vampires, then you suck", which doesn't change the fact that
many good decks are made of all big vampires. And you can say "but if
you planned on not contesting vampires, you wouldn't have randomly sat
down next to someone who randomly also has the same vampire as you",
which doesn't actually work like that), being "screwed beyond the
possibility of getting a single VP" doesn't really describe it. You
don't even get to get a minion out before you are likely ousted (spend
20 pool and 20 transfers on one minion all the while even a completely
low impact predator can likely oust you).

> To me it looks more like the problem is on your side.

Did you even read the start of this thread? Do you know what the
premise is?

-Peter

Messages.Author: the HZA
Messages.Body:
On Jul 12, 2:56 pm, Peter D Bakija <p...@lightlink.com> wrote:

> "If two (or more) copies of a unique minion are in play, both are
> flipped over and considered out of play. During each player's untap
> phase, they must pay a pool to flip over their copy of the minion into
> play (and flip over their opponent's copy out of play) and may use the
> vampire as normal until their opponent does the same on their untap
> phase. They may choose to not pay a pool and burn their copy of the
> minion immediately.

I think if there were a refund on blood counters on your contested
vampire, that would negate enough of the game-destroying effect of
contesting a large or vital vampire.

"When a player chooses to yield a contested vampire, that player
may move all the blood counters on that vampire to his or her pool."

This doesn't remove the possibility of extended contesting, but it
does give players a chance to get their pool back and hopefully
get out another vampire. Even in the scenario being repeated in
this thread, where you have 10 counters on your 11 cap all-star,
and then another player plays that all-star, you can choose to
contest for one turn and then yield, getting all 10 counters back
immediately and in time for your following influence phase.

This does not solve the problem of "If I don't have All-Star Vamp,
I can't play this deck." I believe that if you put all your
deckbuilding
eggs in one basket, you take the consequences of having that
basket smashed with a baseball bat.

I don't believe the current contestation rules need any changes.
I empathize with having your deck screwed over and 1/3 of your
pool tied up, but Pentex and Sense Dep already discourage the
overplacement of eggs in baskets. These are the risks you take.

--hza

On Jul 15, 11:49 am, Ross Ridge <rri...@csclub.uwaterloo.ca> wrote:
> It's not completely random like Peter has said many times.

In a purely mathematical sense, you are correct. Some things are more
likely than others--in any given game, you are more likely to see,
say, Anson (as he is really good and often the basis for many decks as
well as being a good utility player in general) as you are, say, Uriah
Winter (as he is really bad and rarely shows up except in very weird
corner case decks). And in a given play environment, some minions are
more common than others (for example, Asif only has 3 or 4 playable
decks at any given time, and one of them always includes Enkidu. Thus,
there is a roughly 1 in 4 chance of Enkidu showing up in any game I
play with Asif). Yes. Correct.

But in a general sense, if I sit down at a game with a random field of
players with a random field of decks, that someone in a given game is
playing the same minion as me and happens to draw that minion, is
close enough to a totally random occurrence so as to not be worth
worrying about the less random parts. Certainly for a discussion about
"Is the penalty for contesting an important minion appropriate,
considering how random it happens to be"?

> Acknowledged, but its implications ignored.

No, they aren't ignored. Yes. It is certainly possible/likely that the
original designers said "Huh. The contestation rules are a good
failsafe in case certain minions are too strong or people are too
predictable...", and as such, the harsh penalty was measured in
specifically to make people afraid of it. But as the pool of vampires
gets bigger and bigger, and the likelihood of contesting even the
strongest of minions gets smaller and smaller, I'm getting less and
less convinced that the benefit to the current contestation rules
(i.e. a failsafe against overpowered minions, for ex.) outweigh the
negatives to the game (i.e. it occasionally totally screws you in a
completely unfun way, even when you are using a totally un-overpowered
minion).

> For vampire contesting to be anywhere near "completely random",
> then given the number of crypt cards published, it also has to be an
> extreamly rare occurance.

It is extremely rare. To be in a situation where:

A) Contestation is even a possibility.

and

B) It matters.

And yet it still happens sometimes. And when it does, it is often
leads to an incredibly lame and unsatisfying loss/demolishing of a
whole game. Due to pure chance.

-Peter

I think that there are (at least) two senses in which the word
'random' is being used in this thread. One is 'unpredictable', which
is close-ish to the probability sense of the word. Something that is
random in this sense can be more or less likely, uniformly or
otherwise distributed, etc. The other sense is 'unlikely', which is a
more colloquial usage. (As, in, "Dude, that was totally random! Did
you see that?") In this sense, something that is unlikely to happen
or happens very rarely is described as 'random' (even if no random
factors were involved in its occurrance). But for purposes of this
discussion, the latter sense is pretty much a subset of the former,
and essentially includes some assumptions about the distribution and/
or frequency of the randomness.

So, having the possibility to contest _any_ vampire is governed by
random factors. But to some, contesting Anson or Lutz or Arika is
less 'random' than contesting Rex or Lucretia or Patrizia, by which
they mean that it has a higher probability of occurrence. (Or,
alternatively, rolling '00' on percentile dice is 'more random' than
flipping a coin and getting 'heads'.) You can't really measure a
degree of randomness in the former, mathematical sense; you can
measure a probability of occurrence. I know that this has been
commented on explicitly in places in the thread, but I'm pretty sure
that the usage issue is still muddling things.

> Of course, the point he's trying to make is still hung up on the

For the record, I hate those. =) For one, changing the influence
rules to allow you to move blood more easily between uncontrolled
minions is kind of scattershot... to help avoid contestation issues,
you end up changing a bigger part of the game with effects on all
kinds of things. Then if you try to narrow the focus by adding
stipulations, it just becomes too convoluted. The reveal and dump
method just seems like it adds something weird that wasn't there
before. I dunno, it's kind of nebulous, but I just don't like the
"feel" of it. The other suggestion (from James, I think), that when
yielding, you can move any blood on the vampire to your pool seems a
little better. However it seems to remove most of the danger from
contesting and seems wrong flavor-wise.

> though, of course I like
> mine as well.  Thanks for noticing mine and trying to discuss it (and
> the others).
>

I like your variant (both vampires stay controlled; you must pay to
contest or else yield; contesting vampires may not "interact", meaning
that one cannot react while the other is acting, they may not direct
actions at each other, and they may not enter combat with each other
(as if they were minions controlled by the same methuselah); they hold
a sub-referendum to determine how their votes are cast) because it
seems most in keeping with the story of the game. Similarly to how
one methuselah can control minions who might be at odds with each
other (like clan and anti-clan, frex) - just because those minions are
acting in the best interests of the controlling methuselah doesn't
mean that they are friends or are even aware that they're on the same
team. For the same reason, it makes sense to me that two methuselahs
can both be influencing the same minion and trying to guide his
actions to best suit their own agenda - the minion need not be aware
of the influence and is simply acting in what he regards as his own
best interests, but due to conflicting aims of the methuselahs he's
controlling, he may take actions to further both methuselahs' aims.

It makes sense to me even *more* than the current contestation rules,
because I don't really understand how two methuselahs can try to
influence the same vampire and the vampire is just "out of play." It
has the added benefit that it's not terribly complex, and also solves
the "problem" that was set forth by the OP.

Peter's original proposal fits in a similar way, although there's some
unbalance in the case of who gets to have the minion for more time
around the table and the point of sometimes the vampire is more useful
during your own turn and sometimes more useful during others' turns.
It also seems confusing that one vampire can be "protected" by being
out of play, like if there's a Baltimore Purge played, or something
like that. All-in-all, I think it would work out just fine, but it's
not my favorite.

LSJ's proposal uses an existing mechanic (banishment - although maybe
mechanic is the wrong word? game concept?) to resolve the
contestation. It has some benefits as well - it's also reasonably
simple, and being able to transfer off the vampire in order to
gracefully yield is a plus (which I know I said felt a little "wrong"
in James' method, but I think that's more due to it being
instantaneous in that case).

Obviously, there's still the question of whether it would be worth
changing the existing contestation rules. I think it would be, if it
made the game more fun, but since I'm not part of the rules team, it's
just speculation. But being able to use a vampire while still having
to pay to contest it seems like it's most reasonable within the
framework of how the game currently works - there's still a cost for
contestation, but it's not a double-whammy that takes your big cap off
the table temporarily *and* bleeds you dry (or else just takes your
big cap off the table permanently).

For those that say that contestation is around for a reason, and it
encourages deck diversity, I don't disagree, I just have to wonder
whether the minimal encouragement it provides (because of the
unlikelihood of the penalty being enforced) is really enough to
warrant the sledgehammer to the balls that happens when it *is*
enforced.

Which, again, isn't what the folks proposing changes are saying. It's

example that started the thread, Lutz wasn't even key to Peter's
friend's deck - Lutz was just the 11-cap he started working on first,

contestation rules in their present form meaning that if someone by
pure random chance beats you to influencing out a vampire that you may
or may not have cared about when you're halfway through or more,
you've lost turns, pool, and transfers to random chance, and your game
is, if not completely over, at the very least severely handicapped,
whether or not you ever actually contest.

How about this:

Contesting crypt cards works the same as it does now, but the incoming copy (if
it isn't burned for self-contesting) remains in play. When you pay to contest,
your copy re-enters play and the other copy is flipped out of play. When you
yield, the crypt card returns to your* uncontrolled region.

* Where "you" means "the controller's, after breaking any temporary control
effects", as normal.

I think it works a little better than my original suggestion. Simple and very
near to the current rules. The only changes are that the contested card is still
around to use for your part of the table cycle and yielding leaves you with the
card in your uncontrolled region, to siphon blood from or to reinfluence later.

>> near to the current rules. The only changes are that the contested card is still
>> around to use for your part of the table cycle and yielding leaves you with the
>> card in your uncontrolled region, to siphon blood from or to reinfluence later.
>
> I think that version seems to disfavor wall decks in the same way
> Peter's original suggestion does.

Yeah. That part is not unnoticed. But it can't be helped without much more
complexity and then there's always the question of whether it would be worth any
effort at all to ease the life of wall decks.

> However, if (as Peter's been advocating) contesting is as big an issue
> whether or not the actual contest happens (since using several turns
> and poll/transfers in vain is too harsh) then this wouldn't change
> much (or at least only change that for certain type of decks).

Well, obviously, you cannot change how often contesting occurs (or rather, how
often the situation develops in which contesting can occur). That's just deck
construction. Tying any rule to accomplishing that change is just another way of
saying "it's fine. don't change".

And, just as obviously, if the severity of the disability inflicted when the
circumstances that lead to the possibility of contesting occur can be lessened
(that is, make the effect of landing in those circumstances less
game-destroying), then it is better for the game (assuming one finds the
contesting lottery's nuke-pot bad for the game).

The above rule takes the consequences of losing the contesting lottery and
scales them back (perhaps toward reasonableness):

1. Instead of losing the minion altogether, the lottery co-losers split the
minion's table cycle among them (while still paying the 1 pool per cycle cost to
contest).

2. When yielding, the lottery co-loser is able to harvest whats left of xer
original pool investment from the vampire (or can wait until xe is strong enough
to resume the contest).

Those two events: 1) losing the minion (to some degree) and 2) losing the
investment (to some degree) are the things that can be changed. The above
proposal and the other proposals put forward all look at ways to change one or
both of those things, in different degrees (and with varying amounts of complexity).

> This
> also goes against your other suggestion if I remember it correctly,
> since that was to banish the vampires right away when the contesting
> started.

Um. It is a different suggestion. But other than that, it doesn't go against any
other suggestion. My previous suggestion accomplishes changes to the above two
points as well, but to a lesser degree than the above suggestion and with
greater complexity. So you might view the above as an evolutionary step forward
from my previous suggestion. But certainly not against one another.

> Even if the current rules disfavors some deck types (not sure if it
> does, but it's possible) I don't see the point in just changing what
> type gets screwed more.

The point isn't just changing what decks get screwed more, obviously.

The point is lessening the penalty involved in losing the contesting lottery.

time, and have a bunch of pool invested in a minion that will never
see play, and I'll probably be ousted before I see that investment
returned.

The first point is debatable, and the proposed rule wouldn't make life any

even for non-strike-resolution damage) made it harder for some combat decks.

that has little to nothing to do with determining if the change is good for the
game.

Sure. But the things you mention are inherent in the nature of TCGs and are not
changeable. Contesting, on the other hand, is not inherent and is changeable.
And changing the effect it has when it does happen to be more in line with the
rest of the game is a good thing.

Yes. I agree.

under Lady Luck's umbrella a little closer to home so that the game becomes a
little less beholden to the latter effects and a little more about the former
strategy.

You still wind up with all of the above, but with Lady Luck's influence
curtailed a bit.

> [Starting the contest] will still screw us both (a little less depending on what

> minion we're talking about and what xe's supposed to do).

A lot less in most cases (e.g., when the minion is intended to do something to
the prey). For the minion whose sole purpose is to interact on the predator's
turn, yeah, xe'll be almost as screwed in that endeavor as under the current
rules, but xe has other options (like interacting with the prey), which could
still be useful even if it isn't the intended role the vampire was imagined to
have when constructing the crypt.

And then, either you eventually win the contest (better for you, since you've
been able to use the minion a bit in the interim), or you yield (better for you,
since you've had a chance to redistribute any equipment that minion had and now
have a chance to reclaim whatever blood the minion has, and the minion's back in
your uncontrolled region, with any other cards still on him, ready to be brought
out again if you find it advantageous to restart the contest or if the other
copy gets burned or otherwise leaves play).

So no worse even in the worst case and most often better.

> or after I've brought X out and yielded).

Yeah. The effect of not contesting doesn't change. But now the other alternative
(contesting) is more viable, so you won't have to choose to switch to another
vampire as much.

At worst, this comes out to no worse than the current.

On Jul 16, 8:34 am, henrik <www.hen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Sure.
> I'm just one of those that thinks the contesting lottery is as much
> part of the game as the Ventrue vs New Carthage lottery, or the
> Tremere vote vs Malkavian Seven Miseries lottery.

You'll note that blanket clan hosers have seen very little reprinting
(if any, since VTES) and haven't seen any updating/proliferation. As
if the designers decided that clan hosers were just too random. And
that by not reprinting them, or making new versions of them, they are
making the game less prone to random hosing, rather than more prone to
random hosing.

New Carthage, on the other hand, while kind of a clan hoser (in that
it disadvantages Ventrue when it is in play), is much less of a random
occurrence (it isn't in someone's deck just in case they can hose the
Ventrue, like, say, Malk Dementa; it is in someone's deck to help the
Brujah and if it hoses the Ventrue, even better), has a relatively
minor impact (if the Ventrue can't deal with -1 vote per guy, then
they likely weren't voting anyway), and can be killed. Seems like a
reasonable random hosing. If New Carthage said "Ventrue get -3 votes,
-2 bleed, and -1 intercept", that would be not good and a serious
random hosing.

The current contestation rules say "Ventrue get -3 votes, -2 bleed,
and -1 intercept".

> In my world, I guess we could say that there are two parts of the
> game: The part where you play against 3-4 other players and try to
> beat them with stealth/intercept/combat/voting/whatever and the part
> where you play against Lady Luck and try to beat her by minimizing the
> risk of being the victim of a bad library/crypt draw, contesting,
> scissor vs paper seating etc.

Yes. A certain amount of randomness is inevitable in this kind of
game. And a certain amount of planning on it, and trying to game the
environment, and trying to play the odds, is all part of the game. But
in certain situations (like random contestation), the penalty is
simply too big, considering how random the event is, and how little
control the players have over it. Yes, you can make a deck that is
screwed by combat. And if you sit next to a combat deck, you are
probably hosed. But you had a choice to make there, and knew the
risks, and said "well, if I sit next to a combat deck, I'm hosed."
Being in a situation where contestation is a significant issue is not
something you can avoid in the deck building phase. And often not
something you can deal with in the playing the game phase (see: I
spend 20 pool and 6 turns before I have a single minion in play).

I'm not saying that contestation should go away. There still should be
a risk to playing popular/powerful vampires that other folks are
likely to use. There still should be a possibility of negatively
affecting someone's game by strategically contesting their guys.
Contestation is an interesting mechanic that is important to the game.
But the current rules have an effect that is often simply too
devastating and too much of a "you lose the game lottery". Which,
considering how completely random and out of the hands of player's
control it is, is incredibly unfun. Which is why I'd like to see it
get tweaked.

My original suggestion? Probably not the best. But a starting point.
LSJ's "you just get uncontrolled" is very reasonable. I like the "if
you give up a contestation, you get all the blood on that guy put in
your pool" (like a wandering Golconda, kind of)--doesn't fix
everything, but is simple and fixes a lot. LSJ's new suggestion (a
fusion of my idea and his idea) is probably the best, but also the
most complicated.

-Peter

I think it is the case that even in games based on randomness, having
less arbitrary total hosing than more is pretty much always going to
be a worthwhile goal. Like, in poker, which is a game based on a great
deal of randomness, the most popular version is the one where a great
deal of randomness as is removed (see: Texas Hold'em). And Poker could
have rules like "If you draw QH and 7D, you lose!" (like Cups!), but
it doesn't. 'Cause even in games governed by chance, minimizing random
hosing is generally a good thing.

VTES is a game with randomness. Yes. But having fewer ways to randomly
and arbitrarily get shut out of the game seems to be, and have been,
and overall goal for the designers. I mean, *you* might like VTES if
it had a rule where at the start of each game, everyone draws a card
off the top of their deck, and the person (or people) who have the
card that comes first alphabetically loses 15 pool (and heck! You can
even plan for it! Build your deck with only cards that start with the
letters X, Y, Z!). But I suspect that most people would not.

> And after all, I do believe that you're bound to get screwed by the
> randomness every now and then. Be it due to contest or to a second
> turn War Ghoul from your prey.

The second turn War Ghoul from your prey is something that you can
plan for--have combat defense in your deck. Or Entrancement. Or
whatever. The contestation is not. Do you at least see the conceptual
difference there? If you are screwed by second turn War Ghouls (or
whatever), that is the result of a choice you made when building your
deck. If you are screwed by someone having the same minion as you,
that is the result of the completely unreasonable choice you made to
have minions in your deck.

> You win some and you lose some, that's how the game goes. Contesting
> is a small thing that can cause you to lose a table. I'm fine with
> that considering the gains I see from the current contest rules when
> compared to the alternatives.

We haven't seen the alternatives. And if the alternatives make, for
the majority of people involved, the game slightly more fun for being
less prone to random arbitrary hosing due to brutal contestation
(without otherwise significantly injuring the balance of the game),
that strikes me as a good direction to go in.

Clearly, you think otherwise. There you go.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Aaron Clark
Messages.Body:
Peter, another way to fix the problem you're talking about would be to
play with an open uncontrolled region.

When everyone's uncontrolled region is visible for everyone else to
see, it is instantly obvious whether two Methusalehs have a chance of
contesting a vampire. If you both have Lutz in your opening crypt
draw, the Methusaleh going first will not be surprised when his prey
gets Lutz out first. There would be no particular reason to change
the contestation rules since the circumstance you're talking about
would be completely foreseen.

Playing with an open uncontrolled region would have a major change on
how players act in the first few turns. The rule would affect only a
few cards ruleswise, such as Harrod. Playing with an open
uncontrolled region would also:

- remove any doubts about the legality of effects that target cards in
the uncontrolled region.
- make it physically easier to manipulate cards and blood counters
since the counters would not have to be removed from the card when it
leaves the uncontrolled region and flips over.

Seeing other Methusalehs' uncontrolled region would help strengthen
strategy over chance, since you would be able to gauge other players'
strategies from turn one and start acting appropriately. It would
also weaken the disadvantage of having fewer transfers as player 1, 2,
or 3 since your prey can't surprise you as much.

-Aaron Clark

>

Huh. I thought this post was about when you place counters on a
vampire during your minion phase, but someone else gets out that
vampire first so you've lost a lot of turns. It seems like a lot of
the discussion is really about the vulnerabilities of star vampire
decks.

I don't see how anyone will get completely hosed if everyone's
uncontrolled regions are open. If two people are playing a star
vampire deck with the same vampire, the amical way to decide is the
person who starts later gets the vampire and the one who starts
earlier influences out his second-stringers. The un-amical way to
decide is for the person who goes earlier to knowingly contest the
vampire.

VTES does have unique cards, after all. Do you really think it will
ever be changed to allow players to control the same unique card at
the same time? I don't.

Star vampire decks will always have this vulnerability one way or
another. It seems like a good idea to put in a couple of copies of a
younger second-stringer vampire into your crypt who can still use most
of the cards the star can use so your game might not be completely
hosed if you lose access to your star.

adapted to. The designers of the game seem to agree with me here.

> The Baali thing is the most relevant here for me. And yes, that was a
> change that I think made the game (at least a small part of it)
> better.

And yet people thought those rules were fine too. And all sorts of
folks were like "We don't need to change those rules. They are fine."
and all "Changing those rules might make things worse!". And yet...

> And as for the current rules making some decks suffer more than
> others, I'd like an example (other than the obvious example that crap
> decks suffer more than good decks). I don't see any direct way that a
> certain type of decks are hurt more than any other type by the current
> rules.

Decks that rely on big vampires are considerably more hindered by
contestation than decks that rely on small vampires. Decks that rely
on specific minions are considerably more hindered by contestation
than decks that rely on interchangeable minions. Decks that tend to
tool up a single minion (i.e. No Secrets from the Sniper Rifle or wall
of Raven Spies or Someone gets an Assault Rifle) are considerably more
hindered by contestation than decks where no particular minion is any
better than any others at doing what you need to do. The current
incredibly debilitating contestation rules incentivize decks where
contesting a particular minion will be particularly troublesome. Which
encourages people to avoid particular decks (and by "particular", I
mean, "an awful lot of deck strategies"). Which means that the
contestation rules are shooting deck diversity in the foot.

If the contestation rules were less debilitating, this would be less
of the case.

> Maybe. I haven't seen any suggestion that doesn't lessen or remove
> that ability though.

"If you give up contestation, all the blood on that minion is returned
to your pool."

This still allows you to strategically contest a minion, have it leave
play, and have contestation go on as normal. Except if they give up
that minion, they aren't totally out of their whole investment (unless
they already used their pool investment through pulling the blood back
or playing cards or something).

"If you bring a unique minion into play that is already in play, the
one already in play is moved to the uncontrolled region."

This allows you to strategically remove a minion from play until it
comes back to play. If it is low on blood, it might be out of play
forever. Opening up all sorts of clever "I get all the blood off your
guy and then contest him" tech.

Do both of these lessen the penalty of having a minion contested?
Sure. That is the whole point. Do they remove the ability to
strategically contest a minion where it is beneficial to you and
detrimental to your foe? No. It just makes it work differently.

-Peter

Indeed, the rules for transferring back off your vampires were
implemented to allow players to not feel forced to contest. (As in,
I've put 8 counters on this copy of Sheldon and you've brought yours
out, and I couldn't transfer counters back - no mechanism to do so - so
I put an extra one on to contest yours.)

Garfield says:

I nearly lost faith in the concept [of contesting] after people had
noticed so many conflicts, and the effect of a contested card was so
dramatic and often decisive to the game. Skaff Ellis convinced me
it was too good a tool to discard, because how can a player assemble
an always-winning deck when she can't even rely on her vampires
being hers when all the smoke clears?
...
The fact that two players lost the whole game if their powerful
vampires were contested bothered many players, and I eventually
became convinced that it was a problem. I don't mind arbitrary
swings of fate in games, but not such large ones in long games. Tom
Fontaine, or someone in his playtest group, came up with the idea of
withdrawing influence from an uncontrolled vampire.

This was an excellent solution because two players are still hosed
if their big vampires are contested, but at least one of those
players can be righteously angry at the other for not withdrawing
blood rather than plowing ahead and contesting the vampire.

It's interesting that Garfield notes that "two players lost the whole
game" - which is more or less what we're saying, 15 years later.

I think, however, that the impression I get from the early writings is
that the extremes weren't pushed. Just as it appears that no-one put
together decks with 20 copies of Majesty in, I get the impression that
crypts were a diverse set of vampires. Therefore, you bringing out
Anneke and me bringing out Anneke would be because one of my perhaps 2
copies of Anneke came into my uncontrolled region, and the same with
you. The idea of forcing a single vampire strategy through crypt
stacking doesn't seem to be the case - I imagine that you were expecting
a quite different uncontrolled region each time.

It's this that means that Garfield's proposed fix - righteous
indignation - doesn't work when both players need the same vampire. You
might be righteously indignant at me, but I need Anson for my deck and
you need Anson for your deck, or each deck simply doesn't work.

I don't think we're going to be able to wean people off single vampire
strategies (where one vampire is so key, even if there are a hoard of
weenie fans, or something). At least, not this side of the heat death
of the universe. People like them because they're often fun.



> librarian wrote:

> > suggestion.  Most simple, most seems to represent what "contesting" or
> > "uniqueness" would represent in the "real world".
>
> How about this:
>
> Contesting crypt cards works the same as it does now, but the incoming copy (if
> it isn't burned for self-contesting) remains in play. When you pay to contest,
> your copy re-enters play and the other copy is flipped out of play. When you
> yield, the crypt card returns to your* uncontrolled region.
>
> * Where "you" means "the controller's, after breaking any temporary control
> effects", as normal.
>
> I think it works a little better than my original suggestion. Simple and very
> near to the current rules. The only changes are that the contested card is still
> around to use for your part of the table cycle and yielding leaves you with the
> card in your uncontrolled region, to siphon blood from or to reinfluence later.

I definitely like returning to uncontrolled instead of burning, since
it makes the penalty for losing a contest much lower. One of the
reasons that contests are so painful under the current rules is that
once you're in one, it's too costly to give up.

The idea of alternating control seems good for cross-table contests,
but for predator-prey contests (which happen most often in my
experience), it's much worse for the prey than the current rules. In
the proposal above, when I'm contesting with my prey I pay a pool to
get a vamp and deprive my prey of a vamp. In the current rules, I pay
a pool and both of us are deprived our vamp. Also, under the proposed
rules, when I start contesting, it takes a whole round before I get
any use, while the other player gets to use the vamp the entire round.

I like this better:
Exactly like the current rules, but instead of burning the vamp when
you yield, you burn 1 blood on the vamp and return it to your
uncontrolled region.

That way, if you yield, you can get back your investment, but the prey
doesn't get screwed. Also, this is a very small change, and I think
smaller changes are generally better. Finally, I think the current
rules do cause people to consider whether or not they want to play
Arika, Lutz, Una, etc. The chances of contesting those vamps are
still small, but I've seen Arika contested a lot more than I've seen
Nakova, Advocate of Golconda.

Ira

not fundamentally opposed to the idea of contestation. I just think

That is a possibility. I'm currently siding with the "if you yield
contestation, move all the blood on that vampire to your pool" idea.

contestation dynamic (just how much pool you lose for losing your
guy). Doesn't require any extra explanation as to how different rules
affect non minions (i.e. "if you yield contestation, burn your copy of
the card. If that card is a vampire, move all the blood on that
vampire to your pool.") I'm not sure how it would interact with the
Imbued, but that is easy to clarify. I mean, not as interesting as
some sort of alternating control, and superstar decks still take it in
the junk. But a simple, non complicated fix is often the best option.

Correct, that is one reason: lack of sufficient reason to investigate
alternatives to the way library cards are contested. Indeed, that is likely the

Another reason, though, is that controlling a Soul Gem is not a matter of
exerting influence to convince the Gem to do your bidding, it's a matter of

concept, but again that doesn't match the concept used for playing the card in
the first place, and the card still falls under the primary reason above, too.

Ah, I just read this more carefully. Is this the intended design:

Meth A has Arika. Meth C contests. A's Arika goes out of play, and
Meth C's Arika remains in play. Meth A pays a pool, takes actions
with Arika. Meth C yeilds, pays nothing, and on his influence phase
brings Arika into play again, causing A's Arika to go out of play.
Meth A must pay a pool again on his turn.

Therefore, at the cost of tying up pool on Arika, Meth C can cause
Meth A to lose Arika for part of the cycle around the table and pay 1
pool per turn to contest. Maybe that cost is still sufficient, since
tying up all that pool is non-trivial, and Arika could lose blood on
her between the end of Meth C's turn and the start of Meth A's turn.

I still think this proposal is worse than the current rules in the
case of a pred-prey contest, since the pred will get to act with their
star minion while the prey cannot defend. I think moving both to the
uncontrolled region (less 1 blood) is simpler and isn't worse than the
current rule regardless of prey-pred-grandprey-etc relationship.

attempt to imagine what you are seeing here:

-Player A has Anarch Convert and Anarch Revolt.
-Player B has Anarch Convert

During Player A's turn, he pays to contest (assuming alternating
control) Anarch Convert. He gains control of Anarch Convert. He then
does not take damage from Anarch Revolt.

During Player B's turn, he pays to contest Anarch Convert. He gains
control of Anarch Convert. He then does not take damage from Player
A's Anarch Revolt.

(assuming no other Anarchs in play, which is not a really reasonable
assumption, but I'll go with it) lose pool from the Anarch Revolts.
With alternating control, they both don't take damage from Anarch
Revolts. Seems perfectly reasonable to me.

Sure. But running into 10 Oath of Loyalties is something you can plan
on avoiding (i.e. don't play Assamites. Not an optimal solution, but
it's there), is something that doesn't completely end your game when
it accidentally hits the table (you don't care if you can't bleed him
if you are just gonna blow up all his guys...) and can be dealt with
when it is on the table (you can burn them. At stealth. 'Cause you are
Assamites). I realize that it was just a kind of silly example, but
even then, cards like that don't simply end your game randomly,
generally speaking.

Contestation issues are not something you can plan for (other than by
not, ya know, using minions) and can completely end your game before
it even starts when they come up. Which, for my money, is something
worth fixing, where Oath of Loyalty is not.

> But I don't think anyone would consider that to be a good argument for
> changing anything.  If contesting superstars (which I'm personally
> partial towards playing) is such a rare occurrence, how does it rise
> to the level of warranting a change, especially when we could extend
> ad infinitum similarly game-wrecking rare occurrences?

'Cause Contestation is a different kind of game wrecking rare
occurrence than most of the other ones--it is completely and utterly
random, and isn't something you can avoid in deck construction. You
have no control over whether or not your game is ruined from turn 1 by
random contestation issues. You do have control over whether or not
your game is ruined from turn 1 by random seating issues (do you not
want to be wrecked by randomly sitting next to combat? Have combat
defense. Do you not want to be wrecked by randomly sitting next to
intercept? Have stealth. Or whatever.) Random contestation issues are
not something you can control ever.*

*Ok, you can play all Aabt Kindred or Fidai. But if you play all
Fidai, then you are opening up getting killed by 10 Oath of
Loyalties...

-Peter

other "Vampire X" decks, is random and uncontrollable. Still, whether
you'll end up at the same table as one (or more) combat decks, is
equally random and uncontrollable.
What you have control over is the same in both situations though. The
way your deck looks. So either both things are totally random and
uncontrollable, or neither is.

You can build a deck which isn't relying 100% on having a certain
minion in play. You can build a deck where the second minion can get
influenced out rather fast in case something happens to your first. Of
course, there are no fool proof way to protect (except, as you said,
playing Aabbt and stuff like that). You might not get enough crypt
acceleration to bring up your second minion fast enough, you might end
up with 4 copies of your star vampire in your starting crypt etc.
However, the same goes for anti combat. You can add Obedience/Majesty/
Earth Meld/Alpha Glint/Skin of Steel/Bloodform/whatever, but there's
still a (random) risk that you won't have one of those cards in your
hand if you get rushed and trapped by a second turn War Ghoul.

I'm not trying to get into the debate about what's more random than
the other, or what you can have better/worse protection from. But
don't keep saying that there are no ways in hell to plan ahead for
eventual contestation. There are plenty, and they can reduce the risk
of contesting quite much (tbh you don't even need to agree that
they're plenty, just that they exist as much as the ways to protect
you from combat).

impression that saying "Hmm. I won't use Anson, as I don't want to

you end up being in a situation where you can contest minions. It is

Correct.

star) vampire. It is possible to do that.

be somewhat vulnerable to contests. That's the thing about uniqueness
and contesting. Some decks will be more vulnerable though (either
because they try to exploit a certain vampires powerful ability, or
because they don't have any means to survive if their first minion
would be contested), but how vulnerable your deck is to contestation
is very much controllable.

> unique minions. Which isn't something you can realistically do (again,
> excepting Aabt Kindred/Fidai/Tupdog)

The only way to completely avoid it yes. But it's not the only way to
avoid having your entire game screwed because of a contest.

> > star) vampire. It is possible to do that.

> deck diversity by limiting deck diversity".

Nope. You should probably have guessed since that quote doesn't come
from me though.

My main point about contestation is that it exists to balance out the
most powerful crypts.
But in the way that the most powerful minions gets a bit more
balanced, and in the way that a deck built purely on big, fat minions
will be weaker than a deck with a more diverse crypt (in terms of
contest vulnerability), contestation does promote deck diversity. And
making contestation less harsh will change that.

Then again, the risk of contesting is small even with the most
powerful vampires. In my mind though, that's just one more reason not
to change the rules.

And of course, contestation does limit deck diversity in some ways.
But overall I'm fairly sure that it does more to promote deck
diversity than limiting it.

Messages.Author: Bill Ricardi
Messages.Body:
Having read the 300+ messages in this rather... if-you-can't-say-
anything-nice-don't-say-anything-at-all thread, I've come to this
conclusion:

Contesting does indeed suck. However, contesting SHOULD, indeed, suck.
It is a tax and a punishment for those who aren't original enough to
play something other than the flavor of the month. 'Random' contesting
is (and should be) so unbelievably rare given the game's card pool,
that the random punishment doled out is fairly minor.

I'd be for ignoring the contesting rules in draft environments, given
the more limited card pool. Other than that, carpe contestium!

The moral of this thread: Stop playing net decks, stop playing what
the herd considers the 'best and brightest', and you will avoid the
issue of contesting 99.9 percent of the time. Problem solved.
