Now I've read and read and read this thread and I think I atleast
should show some support for the things Henrik have been saying. So,
I'm not trying to add much by this post. I'm mostly just trying to
show my support.

Firstly I must say that it's hilarious that it all started by Lutz
being contested, Lol!

V:tES is a game that include alot of random elements and to be a good
player/deckbuilder you need to be able to handle that. This you can do
in alot of different ways considering V:tES is an awesome game that
have added things like dealing and x-table buddies etc to our arsenal.

I think my most important point when it comes to this thread is that
changing the contest rules would be a bad idea. It won't affect most
casual games since in casual games since you usually make sure you
don't play the same starvamp deck as your friend in a casual game,
atleast not in the playgroups I play with. Basically it would help
decks that are just plain miserable (that can't handle the odds) and
it would help decks like the dem weenie which is already cornercase
broken. The latter needs no help and the former needs to be terminated
as quick as possible to not fuck up the balance of the table anyway.

So, Peter, I saw that you where trying to hijack the thread with Erols
twd regarding this and you're right. It is a good exaple. Problem is
that you're plain wrong (IMO) when it comes to your thesis that that
deck would be screwed by a contest. I'm not saying it wouldn't suck.
I'm just saying there are multiple things you can do, if a contest
happens, to solve the situation. Especially since you know that if you
bring a crypt like that to a big event you'll probably end up risking
contest in atleast 1 game.

Just to mention a few things you could do to avoid the 0 vps. You
could talk your opponent into not contesting at all, you could talk
whoever loses the most from the contest balancewise to help you kill
off the one you contest with, you could bring out a second vampire and
parity shift the one you contest with, etc... Well, point is that you
always have options if you've built a good deck.

Sure, you can take the risk of building a 12x Cybel CtGB deck. But my
opinion on that is that if you play 12x the same strong and fairly
common vampire you probably deserve it. Just like I risk getting 0/6
if I bring a dominate weenie to a tournament with alot of decks that
features alot of x-table interaction.

Well... I just keep rambling now. Most things have already been said
in this thread already. So to sum up. Don't change the rules for a
cornercase situation which usually screws the game for players who
haven't one their pre-tourney and deckbuilding homeworks. It's not
worth opening that Pandoras box and risk unblanacing a stable CCG for
such a cornercase thing.

Regards
Alex

As a player/judge/observer, yeah.

> As I wrote elsewhere in this thread, my experience tells me that the
> most common contesting is expendable weenie/midcaps. In those cases
> it's tough, but very much survivable.
> Second most common would be Arika, Anson, Lutz and other power
> vampires.

The small ones are actually contested more often, I guess. But the frequency
with which the decision to contest comes up is about the same (perhaps more for
all-stars like Arika over other individual choices of crypt cards, but
capacity-wise it occurs, I imagine, on about the same distribution as the
capacity of available crypt cards -- or at least on the distribution of actual
crypts as a whole). And, of course, when the decision comes up, the effects of
each of the choices available (contest or avoid contesting) are more severe, on
average, as the capacities go up.

> You're quite probably visiting (and overlooking) more tournaments than
> me though.
>
>> See also the example "ousted if you start with 7 masters in hand" rule.
>> Unbelievably rare, but that rarity doesn't make the punishment doled out "minor".
>
> In the long run, the punishment could be considered "minor" even if it
> actually did screw your game so hard that you had no chance to play at
> all. It probably won't happen more often than 1/500 games at most, so
> I think "minor" would be a kinda appropriate term.

Minor is appropriate when talking about the level of effect the rule (or any
alternate version of the rule) has on the game as a whole, yes.

But it isn't appropriate when describing the severity of the penalty *when* it
is applied (or when it comes up).

And, as questions go, the question: can an adjustment be better for the game as
a whole (although it won't affect most games -- since the contesting rules for
crypt cards don't affect most games)? is a pretty good one to examine. Make the
game better in the cases in which it comes up without affecting the game (good
or ill) in the cases in which it doesn't.

Garfield thought so: that's why there are rules for using influence to retrieve
pool counters from uncontrolled vampires at all. That rule exists only because
the effect of being put into a position where contesting is an option is
unnecessarily harsh without it.

So. Did that rule go far enough? Perhaps not.

Why make it cost 2 instead of 1?
Or let it "cost" the vampire in question instead of influence (i.e., you can
retrieve all the blood on the uncontrolled vampire by burning that vampire)?

And why only mitigate the cost pre-contest?

(Answer: because that is the portion of the problem completely "random" -- that
is, completely out of the player's control once xe sat down at the table).

But why make the decision to yield so painful as to rush a player to a lost
position (and remove any strategic element the game might offer for that player)?

You could adjust the rules so that either (or both) the decision to yield is
less game-destroying or the decision to continue to contest is less
game-destroying, increasing the strategic value of the contesting angle of the game.

Like by some sort of shared-control-on-contesting rules. Or
blood-recoup-on-yielding rule.

> If it happens very
> often that you find yourself in a situation where contesting is a
> problem, it's probably your own fault (bad meta gaming, bad deck
> building etc.)

Yes. No one claims that it occurs often for anyone, problematically or otherwise.

> In an single game though, the severeness of the punishment is mostly
> dependent on deck building and/or table talking skills (with some luck
> involved, as always).

It is affected somewhat by that, yes. But for many decks (which are not
themselves "bad" decks to be punitively affected by the rules just to make
players decide to play them less), the severity choices range from "very bad"
to "very very bad". A question is: would "merely bad" or "strategic risk" be
good to have as options instead?

> And, as questions go, the question: can an adjustment be better for the game as

> or ill) in the cases in which it doesn't.

I consider the effect the rule has on deck diversity to make the game
better than it would be without that effect (or with a weakening of
that effect). So it's not just about making the game outright better
by adjusting the "penalty" for contesting.

> Garfield thought so: that's why there are rules for using influence to retrieve
> pool counters from uncontrolled vampires at all. That rule exists only because
> the effect of being put into a position where contesting is an option is
> unnecessarily harsh without it.

Not to disrespect Garfield, but he also thought giving dominate G:tU,
Conditioning and Deflection was good :s

> So. Did that rule go far enough? Perhaps not.
>
> Why make it cost 2 instead of 1?
> Or let it "cost" the vampire in question instead of influence (i.e., you can
> retrieve all the blood on the uncontrolled vampire by burning that vampire)?

What it does now is to balance out the effect of cards like Govern the
Unaligned, Fourth Tradition: The Accounting etc, especially when
combined with multi acting. For example, using three actions with 1-3
cap 4 vampire to add 9 blood counters to a 3 cap vampire, burning it
and transferring out a 6 cap for that blood. Stuff like that is one
thing to consider at least.
I'm not sure why 2 was the magic number for Garfield though, but I
don't really see how that would matter either. Personally I think the
contest rules are more important today than it was 15 years ago, since
net decking is more common and somewhat limited by contest risks.

> But why make the decision to yield so painful as to rush a player to a lost
> position (and remove any strategic element the game might offer for that player)?

Strategic elements are still there, with the exception of the
contested minion. Playing master cards, table talk, using your other
minions etc.
And I'm still not convinced that yielding a contest leads you to a
lost position, at least not if your deck was built to be able to
handle the loss of a minion.

> You could adjust the rules so that either (or both) the decision to yield is
> less game-destroying or the decision to continue to contest is less
> game-destroying, increasing the strategic value of the contesting angle of the game.

I'm not sure how the strategic value of contesting would increase by
making it easier.

> Like by some sort of shared-control-on-contesting rules. Or
> blood-recoup-on-yielding rule.

The shared-control rule has some, imo rather big, issues which has
been mentioned elsewhere in the thread.
Blood-recoup-on-yielding changes the game (better for some, worse for
some) but doesn't do much that a simple announcement of what minion
you're influencing to wouldn't fix as well. (Assuming we're talking
about the early game contest, that is. Later in the game contesting
might be used for strategic reasons, and in those cases I think the
cost of both contesting and yielding is fine).

> > In an single game though, the severeness of the punishment is mostly
> > dependent on deck building and/or table talking skills (with some luck
> > involved, as always).
>
> It is affected somewhat by that, yes. But for many decks (which are not
> themselves "bad" decks to be punitively affected by the rules just to make
> players decide to play them less), the severity choices range from "very bad"
> to "very very bad". A question is: would "merely bad" or "strategic risk" be
> good to have as options instead?

In one way, it would perhaps be good to have those options. But then
again, certain sleazy decks would become more viable if contesting was
less of an issue. Dementation weenies are a pretty good example of a
deck that most likely would be played more often if contesting wasn't
as hard as it is today.

In the end, I'm not totally blind to that a change of the current
rules could possibly bring something good. I just think that what such
a change would remove as well, is worth more. At least with the
suggestions seen so far.

On Jul 20, 8:40 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

> Bill Ricardi wrote:
> > Contesting does indeed suck. However, contesting SHOULD, indeed, suck.
> > It is a tax and a punishment for those who aren't original enough to
> > play something other than the flavor of the month.
>
> What about the two players who get tired of playing the flavor of the month and
> go back to their respective drawing boards and come up with original decks that
> happen to focus on the same obscure and rarely-used vampire?

Already addressed. Given the massive card pool available in the game,
the random contesting situation is rare enough. You're talking about a
one in a thousand situation, where two people think up the same
'obscure and rarely-used' theme and use it at the same time. To that I
say, if you wanted to play a game without the random chance of bad
luck, switch to chess. When you have to come up with a a bizarre
situation that involves the words 'happen to focus on the same obscure
and rarely-used', you should probably re-think the issue..

> > 'Random' contesting
> > is (and should be) so unbelievably rare given the game's card pool,
> > that the random punishment doled out is fairly minor.
>
> Not quite. The random punishment is doled out infrequently, but when it is doled
> out, it is seldom in a minor manner.
>
> See also the example "ousted if you start with 7 masters in hand" rule.
> Unbelievably rare, but that rarity doesn't make the punishment doled out "minor".

Of course it does. You have to think long term.

> > I'd be for ignoring the contesting rules in draft environments, given
> > the more limited card pool. Other than that, carpe contestium!

> Why the exception for draft? By your POV, those players should avoid playing the

> good vampires in the set and instead play the weak ones and the ones that don't
> mix well with the sets being drafted (the draft equivalent of "stop playing net
> decks, stop playing what the herd considers the best"). So as to lower their
> chances of having contestation issues come up.

I already explained why the exception for draft: A more limited card
pool. If that isn't a good enough reason for you, then you don't
understand how to create a good draft environment. VTES is already an
iffy draft game (and if you disagree, let's compare the ratio of draft
to normal product sales in VTES and Magic, shall we?), so it is
reasonable to tweak the rules to make it more enjoyable.

Without a harsh penalty for contesting, all you're doing from a design
point of view is encouraging a narrow tournament pool. From a sales
point of view, you're driving secondary market activity, not primary.
It hurts the game to only have a handful of viable archetypes, and it
drives people away from innovation. If that's what you want, go for it.

On Jul 21, 1:20 am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:

> These situations aren't q requirement. These bizarro-world situations are only
> presented for those people who refuse to look at the issue through the main lens
> of simply making the game better for the cases when it does come up (without
> harming it for when it doesn't).

Except, as I already pointed out, it DOES harm the game to make
contesting less severe. So the rest is moot.

> As for playing chess, the same could be said for the lose-on-seven-masters rule.
>
> Not being completely deterministic is no reason to be overly punitive on matters
> of bad luck.

There's nothing 'overly' punitive about it. Where was this discussion
when there was only 3 or 4 sets? THAT was when you might consider the
contesting rules overly punitive. Now, when the chances of it
happening should be less and less with each new card that is
released... now the discussion is important?

> > Of course it does. You have to think long term.
>
> No.
>
> The random punishment is doled out infrequently, but when it is doled out, it is
> seldom in a minor manner.

And yet, in the scope of what matters in a competitive environment, it
IS a minor matter. If you have a truly good deck, you think in terms
of the three or four rounds it takes to make a final table, not 1
round. You can get hosed by the random contesting in 1 round and still
easily have enough VP's for the final table. In fact, depending on
what is being contested, you might pick up a VP or two in that round
as well!

So yes you DO have to think long term, at least as long as a standard
tournament. That is the unit, that is the yardstick. And if your
quality, non-net deck does happen to have a catastrophic contesting
issue in the final round, then you either weren't as original as you
thought you were, or you are suffering from a bout of very bad luck.
And yet it is still better than sitting down and facing three net
decks stolen right from the TDWA that don't have to worry very much
about contesting with each other.

And if you're not talking about a competitive environment, anyone can
make their own 'house rules' about contesting, so please don't go
there. If we're not talking about an official rules change that
impacts the tournament landscape, then knock yourself out with
whatever 'casual' solution you want.

> > I already explained why the exception for draft: A more limited card
> > pool.
>
> And your rationale for not changing the rule in constructed applies just as much
> to limited, so the exception doesn't hold water under your strictures.

How can you not understand that you will contest a hell of a lot more
in a limited environment, and that your deck construction is often
forced to be much more narrow depending on the 'theme' of the set? Do
you get that, or do you not?

> > VTES is already an
> > iffy draft game (and if you disagree, let's compare the ratio of draft
> > to normal product sales in VTES and Magic, shall we?), so it is
> > reasonable to tweak the rules to make it more enjoyable.
>
> But unreasonable to tweak the rules of constructed to make it more enjoyable?

IF it made it more enjoyable, but as I pointed out, it will make
constructed LESS enjoyable. Do you really, honestly want to see the
same decks over and over again because you watered down the penalty
for contesting? That is what you consider more enjoyable?

> > Without a harsh penalty for contesting, all you're doing from a design
> > point of view is encouraging a narrow tournament pool.
>
> Not at all. Contesting would still carry a penalty, just not an overly-punitive one.

Looking at the TDWA, it is already on the edge of a lack of
innovation, given the massive card pool. That suggests that the
penalty is NOT overly-punitive, or people would diversify more to
avoid the risks. You're suggesting weakening a mechanic that doesn't
need weakening.

> > From a sales
> > point of view, you're driving secondary market activity, not primary.
> > It hurts the game to only have a handful of viable archetypes, and it
> > drives people away from innovation. If that's what you want, go for it.
>
> Strawman. Not even worth the seven characters it takes to say so.

When it comes to the corporate bottom line, there's nothing strawman
about my statement. If you don't want to address sales figures, that's
fine. But there is a reason that other companies register card sales
in the hundreds of millions gross per annum, with player bases
measured in the millions.

The reasons include having a viable draft environment, a unified card
database that has standardized wording with card text that is promptly
updated for all rulings (without using the crutch of 'designer
intent'), and an online version of the product that is so addictive
that it makes money hand over fist, despite its own issues.

Of the problems that need fixing with VTES, contesting rates so low on
the list as to be laughable. Why is this fairly rare issue so
important to you, when there is so much work to be done that can
attract new players and enhance everyone's enjoyment of the game?

10 + 3 is 13 pool + 6 turns (3 to influence and 3 to contest) half
your pool and half the game is gone. Can you self-oust? Sure, all
you have to do is claim that you can't play your game without
Democritus. Would I say that the game is already lost? In most cases,

Since Hector is only 16% of your starting pool versus 33% for

Pentex is removable.
Combat is defensible
Banishment gets more difficult (to the point of impossibility) the
larger your minion is. Also may be blocked or voted down (which your

You can build your deck to defend against all three of these and they

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

I don't know that you have pointed this out to any level that I'm
buying into. How does making contestation have more of a reasonable
penalty harm the game?

Currently, contestation is not enough of a deterrent to prevent people
from playing derivative decks; people play with Anson and Arika and
Dememntation weenies all the time. Making it less severe isn't going
to change this. The rest of the game rules do a much better job of
encouraging deck diversity than the contestation rules do.

That being said, currently, the contestation rules are so harsh so
that in the random and infrequent instances that it comes up, it can
end your game before it even starts. Which, again, doesn't dissuade
people from playing powerful/popular minions (go look at the TWDA. Oh,
wait. You already did.) But does manage to make the game incredibly
unfun a great deal of the time that it randomly comes up.

> IF it made it more enjoyable, but as I pointed out, it will make
> constructed LESS enjoyable. Do you really, honestly want to see the
> same decks over and over again because you watered down the penalty
> for contesting? That is what you consider more enjoyable?

What actual evidence do you have that people don't play the same decks
over and over again because they are afraid of contesting minions? The
TWDA is full of decks that use the same good minions over and over
again. I see the same good minions over and over again. The risk of
contestation is small enough that it does not dissuade using the same
good minions over and over again.

> Looking at the TDWA, it is already on the edge of a lack of
> innovation, given the massive card pool. That suggests that the
> penalty is NOT overly-punitive, or people would diversify more to
> avoid the risks. You're suggesting weakening a mechanic that doesn't
> need weakening.

You are attributing something to a mechanic that it doesn't
necessarily do.

People use different decks in VTES 'cause the game encourages you to
use different decks. Playing the metagame, trying new and interesting
strategies, trying to game the environment. These all encourage people
to use different decks. Fear of contestation? This does not discourage
people from using the same obvious vampires (heck, someone just posted
a TWD that could have been called "Team Most Likely To Be Contested".
The person playing it would not have been using Arika and Marcus Vitel
had he been particularly concerned about the likelihood of
contesting).

-Peter

some sort of survey. The probe was powered by a plutonium radiation
source. The chance of the the rocket malfunctioning and the plutonium
being spread finely into the atmosphere killing all life on the planet
was said to be zero. If it had malfunctioned, though, while it would
have been a very unlikely (or rare - probably singular, even) event,

perspective.

It doesn't necessarily mean that they go to tier 2, and it surely
doesn't drive every player there. Some will end up risking a contest

people will stay in a given "tier").
Other things that can happen instead of players going away from tier

to handle contesting some other way than rolling over

> > one playing the card.
>

> to crypt bloat, it will be worse.

Just to make it clear, are you talking about exchanging the rule where
you can use 2 transfers to bring 1 blood back from an uncontrolled
vampire to your pool? If that's the case, then I can see that you have
a point (even if it also opens up new ways to use GtU for bloating).

to burn/remove a vampire in your uncontrolled region to transfer all

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Jul 22, 7:07 am, henrik <www.hen...@gmail.com> wrote:
> That's because the question is faulty since you're not necessarily
> screwed when you contest a vampire.

Sigh. I had escaped! And then I got pulled back in. I am weak.

You are always somewhat screwed when you contest a vampire, relative
to not contesting a vampire. Always. It is not consistently instantly
game ending screwed, no, but a lot of the time, it is. The issue at
hand, which you keep side stepping, is "Are the penalties for
contesting a vampire overly harsh". Is potentially losing a huge
investment, and one of the important functional aspects of your deck,
and then even more pool on top of that an appropriate penalty for
accidentally sitting down at at table with someone else who randomly
drew the same guy as you?

The guy who *designed the game* admitted that the penalty for
contestation was possibly larger than it should be, and then invented
a rule (un-transferring) to attempt to mitigate the penalty. As time
has gone on, it turns out (at least in the view of many people) that,
yes, the penalty for contestation is probably larger than it should
be, and that the attempt to mitigate that penalty is not sufficient.

Yes. You can build a deck that isn't particularly vulnerable to
contestation (Like by playing all Dementation weenies. Or by not using
huge vampires. Or by not relying on a specific vampire. All of which
significantly limits the kinds of decks you can play...) And you can
attempt to mitigate the negative effects when it comes up through
trying to con people into helping you or whatever. But none of this
has any relevance at all to the question "Are the penalties for
contesting a vampire overly harsh".

And yes, I realize that you believe that they are not. Ok. That is
you. And yes, I realize that I believe that they are. Yes. That is me.
But at least by arguing about the same thing, we might be able to
illuminate the issue, as opposed to just arguing past each other.

> Changing the rules on the
> assumption that contesting automatically leads to a game loss would be
> stupid.

Yes. This is true. Which is why no one is doing that. Changing the
rules on the assumption that the penalties for contesting vampires is
too harsh, however, would not be stupid. Much like it was not stupid
to consider changing the rules on the assumption that 1 point of
aggravated damage being capable of burning a vampire was not stupid.

The penalties for contesting a vampire are too harsh. Are they
automatically game losing? Not always, but sometimes. But they
certainly are overly debilitating, considering how incredibly random
they are. Making the rules for contesting vampires somewhat less harsh
seems like a reasonable option to take.

Alternating control of minions is, admittedly, complicated and weird.
Interesting, but probably too big of a change. Getting all the blood
off of a minion when you yield contestation, however, seems like a
totally reasonable, minor change that would make contestation much
less harsh but without changing it too much. You still lose control of
a minion. You still have a penalty for being contested. If you don't
want to yield the contestation, you end up in the exact same place you
would have with the current rules. You can still "strategically"
contest a minion to remove them from play. If someone has gotten a
bunch of use out of that minion (i.e. spent all their blood already),
they don't get much, if any, return. Any part of the contestation
rules that might encourage people to play less popular vampires is
still there. A penalty for playing more popular vampires is still
there.

-Peter

> "If two (or more) copies of a unique minion are in play, both are
> flipped over and considered out of play. During each player's untap
> phase, they must pay a pool to flip over their copy of the minion into
> play (and flip over their opponent's copy out of play) and may use the
> vampire as normal until their opponent does the same on their untap
> phase. They may choose to not pay a pool and burn their copy of the
> minion immediately."

I think the idea is cool. I might like it a bit better if the effect
you describe cost 2 pool, and 1 pool was merely the cost of not
burning your copy. But maybe that's getting too complex now.

one of those "equalizing" considerations that makes the "good
vampires" less good (though, as you say, the sheer number of vampires

Lucretia. It may well be that the fact that he got contested, and I
did not, was not COMPLETELY random.

I note that this thread is 386 posts long, and I have read virtually
none of them. Forgive if what I say has been said ten times before.

But sure.
If I'm playing a crypt with only high caps (which is a risk,
especially when it comes to contesting) then I make sure to have lots
of crypt acceleration. This helps me to get my first minion out fast,
so that others might not have influenced said minion out before me
(since, in the end, the one who brings out the second copy is usually
the one who brings the contest to the table).
If I'm playing with a star vampire, I start of by thinking about how
big risk there is for contesting that vampire in the upcoming
tournament. If it's a new, really strong vampire I probably chose
another deck since the risk is too high. Do note that I said risk for
contesting, not penalty for contesting. Contesting is worse than not
contesting, and this is a choice I'd make even if the rules for
contesting was changed to something less harsh.
But back to the star vampire scenario. Again, if it's a big minion I
use crypt acceleration. If there are no really good reasons for it,
which there usually isn't, I don't include more high caps than the
actual star vampire. I include weenies/midcaps that are selected by
their abilities to get the deck working somewhat even if I don't get
the star vampire out (or if I end up in a contest). Yes, dominate
weenies that can bounce bleeds are great here (if appropriate to the
rest of the deck) but by far not the only choice. Stick, Bobby Lemon
and Beetleman could work if the star vampire has ANI. I'm sure you can
figure the trick out. Thinking about what clan the supporting vampires
might is also be important if you want to use clan based masters or
so.
There are a couple of ways to lessen the effect of contesting.
Basically, make sure your deck can be played without your star vampire
or if anything happens to the first minion you bring out. Reality is
that lots of things can happen, and which of all the possible things
is kinda hard to foresee. But making sure you can manage without that
vampire is good.

Ira Fay wrote:
> On Jul 21, 3:31 am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
>> "Originally there was no way to retrieve counters from uncontrolled cards. Due
>> to contesting, a way was added. It costs 2 transfers. Why cost 2? Why not cost 1
>> or cost the vampire?"

> Hello LSJ,
>
> Could you reiterate the most promising improvement that you're
> currently considering? I will implement that change in all my JOL and
> non-tournament games moving forward, so that perhaps sometime in the
> next year I might get some playtest data to report.

Well, with the understanding that influence-back rule was added to handle
contesting issues (and has ended up turning Ecoterrorists and superior Govern
and the like into bloat tools instead of the pack-building tools they were
designed to be), I'd say changing something along those lines wouldn't be too
out of line (as long as something's getting changed regarding contesting):

Remove "spend 2 transfers to move 1 counter from a card in your uncontrolled
region to your pool."

Add "remove from the game a crypt card in your uncontrolled region that would
contest a card in play to move all blood counters from it to your pool and draw
a card from your crypt".

And make yielding a crypt card return the crypt card to the permanent
controller's uncontrolled region, for good measure.

Whether it's arbitrary and disproportionate is debatable, I don't
believe contesting is. However, I would say that all bad luck is in
some way rules-driven.

blame

library

those days)

My order of choice would be 1, 3 and number 2 at a very, very last
third place. Same thing goes for contesting, blaming the rules should
always be the last outpost.

The new proposed rule for contestation does nothing to prevent a

Messages.Author: witness1

I feel like rules-based things you do in the influence phase to
manipulate the counters on your uncontrolled minions should generally
cost transfers. Maybe there's no good reason for that except
tradition, but it seems more intuitive.

Things that the rules tell you you can do in your Master phase cost
MPAs, and things that the rules tell you you can do in the Discard
Phase cost DPAs. In phases where the rules don't have a general
restriction (like Untap and Action), you also don't have a currency
with which to use effects. Obviously card text (as on Blood Doll) can
give you something to do that doesn't cost that currency, but it seems
more intuitive that things you can do in one of the abstract-currency
phases _without_ card text would utilize that currency.

-witness1

If there were a rule: "During your untap phase, you get X untap phase actions,
where X is the number of Imbued you control. You may use an untap phase action
to put a Conviction card on an Imbued. An Imbued cannot receive more than one
Conviction card this way each turn." then that would also not preclude the
current rules on untapping cards or gaining a pool for the Edge or paying to
contest.

or moving the gaining pool for the Edge to the master phase (still without using
a master phase action).

I'm certainly not opposed to the idea that sacking the vampire could cost a
transfer or four, but the cost doesn't seem to be an intrinsic need on the part
of the game.

> > way to bloat that doesn't require a master card.
>
> Could be. Then the question becomes: is it a bad change, a good change, or a
> wash (for the game as a whole)?
>
> > I think removing that would do a lot of harm to already existing cards.
>
> I can't think of any.

The ones that spring to my mind are Convergence and to a lesser extent
Bay and Howl. Unlike cards like Govern or Art Museum, these cards move
'one from each' onto a single uncontrolled vampire. In order for these
cards to reach 'strong' usefulness, you need to have more than a few
vampires in play to cull from.. which in turn puts a lot of blood onto
a single vampire. Which in practice is often more than that vampires
capacity, because you packed your deck with smaller vampires so that
you could get them out in droves to cull from... or, in the case of
Covergence, because almost all of the Panders are small to begin with.
And part of the utility of these cards is that you can back-transfer
the blood that's above the capacity of your likely-small crypt
vampire..

So for Convergence, the card would basically boil down to the
following uses after this proposed change:

a) get a bunch of blood onto one of the _very_ few mid-cap Panders in
the entire game

or b) use it to move a very few blood counters onto one of the many
small Panders, because you only have a couple of panders in play so
far

or c) use it to move a very few blood counters onto one of the many
small Panders, and move some more blood counters off of the rest of
your Panders to the blood bank, because they're going to be over-
capacity for the inevitably small target, and you can't bring them
back to your pool.

A is very corner case, what with all of three printed vampires above a
3-cap (plus an advanced vamp).

B is usable, but weak - either you aren't playing many of the clan
for which it is intended, or it's still early-game, and it is likely
weaker than cards like Tribute or Grooming the Protege once you count
the clan requirement

C is usable, but even weaker, as now you're actively spending extra
blood to achieve the same moderate-to-weak result as case B.

(Of course, you could always try to Converge onto a small Pander that
would contest with what you have in play.. but why on earth would you
play a bunch of small Panders and then plan your crypt to Contest
them, when the end result is exactly the same as Tribute to the Master
only without burning an uncontrolled vampire?)

Bay and Howl suffers the same fate, except that A is mitigated a
little by a bigger selection of larger vampires. Of course, if you're
getting enough vampires into play to make the reward worth using on a
bigger vampire, you aren't including many bigger vampires in your
crypt in the first place likely, so you're just hoping that you can
get one of those into your uncontrolled region to avoid being stuck in
category C.

-John Flournoy

On Jul 23, 3:33 pm, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> witness1 wrote:
> > I feel like rules-based things you do in the influence phase to
> > manipulate the counters on your uncontrolled minions should generally
> > cost transfers. Maybe there's no good reason for that except
> > tradition, but it seems more intuitive.
>
> > Things that the rules tell you you can do in your Master phase cost
> > MPAs, and things that the rules tell you you can do in the Discard
> > Phase cost DPAs. In phases where the rules don't have a general
> > restriction (like Untap and Action), you also don't have a currency
> > with which to use effects. Obviously card text (as on Blood Doll) can
> > give you something to do that doesn't cost that currency, but it seems
> > more intuitive that things you can do in one of the abstract-currency
> > phases _without_ card text would utilize that currency.
>
> I don't see it as a given like that.

Oh it's absolutely not a logical requirement. It's just that the way
the phases currently work, if you do something in the Master phase or
the Influence phase or the Discard phase, you are either 1) following
card text or 2) ticking down the currency you could spend in those
phases. There's nothing in those phases that you need to remember that
isn't doing one of those things. So players are primed to think in
those terms, during those phases.

> If there were a rule: "During your untap phase, you get X untap phase actions,
> where X is the number of Imbued you control. You may use an untap phase action
> to put a Conviction card on an Imbued. An Imbued cannot receive more than one
> Conviction card this way each turn." then that would also not preclude the
> current rules on untapping cards or gaining a pool for the Edge or paying to
> contest.

And that would be less intuitive than the actual rules. Not wrong,
unplayable, or even bad. Just less intuitive than an easily available
alternative.

> Likewise, there'd be nothing inherently wrong with discarding down to your hand
> size only during your discard phase (still without using discard phase actions),

Sure. The game went a long time without there even really _being_ a
discard phase action, because the only thing you could do was discard
a single card (barring card text). But it was still a separate phase
for that single purpose instead of just "At the end of the influence
phase, you can discard one card and draw to replace". And I think it
was a separate phase for a reason.

> or moving the gaining pool for the Edge to the master phase (still without using
> a master phase action).

There's nothing wrong with it, but there's a reason that's _not_ the
rule. The reason might be "Richard Garfield wanted you to feel stupid
when you play a Master Card before gaining for the edge," or even "We
never thought of it," but those don't seem any more likely than "We
wanted the Master Phase to be a simple phase where you play and use
Master cards". It doesn't really hurt the game any that (e.g.) Form of
Corruption is burned in the Master Phase, but choosing another phase
could have been more intuitive.

> I'm certainly not opposed to the idea that sacking the vampire could cost a
> transfer or four, but the cost doesn't seem to be an intrinsic need on the part
> of the game.

Well, they are called "transfers" instead of "uploads". It kind of
implies that you can move things around with them (and not necessarily
just one direction). I mean, your method (eventually) costs the 4
transfers (and a pool) to draw a new guy if you want to continue
bloating and/or start using the relevant effects to bring out more
(non-contesting) minions.

-witness1

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

On Jul 24, 9:30 am, Drain <dr...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> Rather than ponder on the uptake for GtU's prospects, I would worry
> about the shift in power-level for cards like Banishment, Exile and
> Reality.

As I understand LSJ's suggestion, it is:

1) You can no longer untransfer blood off uncontrolled minions.

2) If you yield contestation, your contested minion is returned to the
uncontrolled region.

3) You can burn an uncontrolled minion that, if brought into play,
would contest another minion [controlled by another player] and return
all the blood on that uncontrolled minion to your pool.

Yes, this makes using Govern and Eco Terrorists or whatever to bloat
much more difficult (Khalmaky Nightmares for the win!).

So in terms of Banishment, the issue is that if your guy gets
Banished, you can't pull the blood off of them. Which certainly could
be a problem--your prey is low on pool. You Banish their 8 cap who has
4 blood on him. Your prey now is out an 8 cap vampire, can't influence
him back out (as he is too low on pool to spend 4 to get him back out
and reasonably survive), and can't get the blood back off him. That
seems kind of egregiously bad.

Another problem that this rule would introduce is the one that happens
when you have a big minion half influenced, and when things turn for
the worse, you can't then decide to stop influencing him out and get
your pool back. You are stuck with 4-6 pool sitting on a minion that
you can't ever get back. Which seems sub-optimal to me.

I'd suggest retaining the "you can untransfer at 2:1" rule, as that is
something that comes up in every game, and would be a really
significant change to the game (yeah, I also can't really shed a tear
for Govern being downpowered, but I think that would have a lot of
negative impact otherwise). But points 2 and 3 (above) strike me as
perfectly reasonable, and I don't think that point 1 needs to be in
place to make points 2 and 3 work out fairly.

-Peter

I'd also be worried about the potential for self-Banishment[0]. A deck
in trouble has a decent amount of blood on a vampire, banishes it, notes
that the vampire has left play since their last turn, and explodes it in
the uncontrolled region.

This may completely neuter the deck's ability to win (right now), but

cause a game to lull, which I think is likely to be a retrograde step.

from my weenie predator." You have to pile all your pool onto Suhailah

like:

else's controlled minion, you may remove it from the game to move the
counters to:

modifications.

in 3), I mention the Kuta rules since if we're dicking with the
uncontrolled region quite a bit, now seems like a reasonable time to do

Messages.Author: Ira Fay
Messages.Body:
On Jul 23, 11:15 am, LSJ <vtes...@white-wolf.com> wrote:
> librarian wrote:
> > The removal of transferring back is a huge change.  I think it's a good
> > way to bloat that isn't a master card.  Maybe even the best/most common
> > way to bloat that doesn't require a master card.
>
> Could be. Then the question becomes: is it a bad change, a good change, or a
> wash (for the game as a whole)?

I believe we should strive to minimize change to the ruleset, so we
should only make good changes. If it's bad or merely a wash, we
shouldn't make the change. Also, the larger the change, the larger
the risk of unintended consequences.

My understanding of the most recent iteration of the rule is:
You may remove from the game a crypt card that would contest a card in
play to move all the counters on that card to your pool and decrypt.
You may remove from the game a crypt card that was in play since your
last turn to move all the counters on that card to your pool and
decrypt.
Yielding a crypt-card contest returns the card to your uncontrolled
region.
Also, remove the existing rule that you can transfer back 2:1.

Let's not lose sight of the original problem we're trying to fix:
randomly getting hosed by vampire contestation is unfun.

It seems like what is actually happening is that LSJ has also added
the design problem of: Govern the Unaligned (and possibly other bloat
cards) are too powerful (or very close to too powerful.)

Possibly also: Since Govern the Unaligned (and other similar cards)
can be used for bloating, players may use it that way and slow down
the game, instead of trying to oust their prey.

My concerns with the above solution are as follows:
1) It's a very large change that will likely have unintended
consequences. For instance:
- That sort of bloat now requires crypt duplication.
- That sort of bloat will be more difficult, and therefore we will
build decks that bloat in other ways, likely through Masters, which
are less interactive. Blocking and stealthing through those bloat
actions are very interesting.
2) The rule is trying to solve too much at once. If there are
problems with Govern and other similar cards, fix those cards via
Blood Cult Awareness Network and similar cards. Event: When any
Methuselah puts blood from the blood bank on an uncontrolled minion,
put one less blood instead.
3) If you yield at the beginning of your turn, you can contest again
at the end of your turn without transfers. Is merely locking up the
pool on the vamp sufficient for the contest?
4) Other issues that have already been mentioned.

I'd like to stay focused purely on the contestation issue. How about
this for a simple solution:
If you yield a contest for a unique crypt card, move the blood or life
on the minion to your pool, then burn the minion.

That's a very minor change from the current rules, but greatly lessens
the cost of yeilding contest.

Ira

In your opinion.

However, that still does not address the idea that this was a side
effect.

Designer A: "So, this contesting thing. It's a bit of a crock when it
happens and kills two players, don't you think?"
Designer B: "Sure is. How about we let them change their mind?"
Designer A: "What do you have in mind?"
Designer B: "Well, I've got two ideas. In one, you can take all the
counters from a vampire in your uncontrolled region and move
them all to one other vampire in your uncontrolled region."
Designer A: "That sounds interesting. What's the other idea?"
Designer B: "My other idea is that you can pull back pool off vampires."
Designer A: "Mmm, that's interesting too."
Designer B: "Yeah, a feature with this idea is that Art Museum and
Fourth Tradition can become a bit more multi-functional. When
you draw them early on, they can speed you up. When you draw
them later on, they can generate you a bit of pool."
Designer A: "So, Ecoterrorists could help you get a Bomb, in a
roundabout way?"
Designer B: "Yeah, and your Art Museum could help you develop a Society
Hunting Ground, too. Obviously, it wouldn't always work out
that way, but I think the role-players would appreciate that."
Designer A: "What about Fourth Tradition? Three pool is quite a lot to
get in one go."
Designer B: "That's true. Let me think about that..."
Designer A: "Hey, I know, how about we make it a bit slower to pull pool
back? That way, players are still encouraged to make the
'right' decision early on. And then it doesn't give them all
the pool at once. So a player playing Govern the Unaligned
twice in one turn might be able to get six pool, but only, say,
two a turn?"
Designer B: "Wicked. We've got a better handle on contesting vampires,
and come up with some other interesting things for players to
do. Let's suggest this at the next meeting."

Yet, despite no evidence on the Design Team's thinking at all, you
repeatedly assert that this is a side effect. And, further, have just
asserted on IRC that this is a side effect that should be avoided. You
are developing premises based on baseless assertions.

Your so-called evidence on this matter is utterly, utterly meaningless.
It is completely devoid of all merit.



On Jul 12, 2:56 pm, Peter D Bakija <p...@lightlink.com> wrote:
> So as we were driving back from the New York Qualifier last night,
> during the post game analysis of my pal Ben's crashing and burning with
> what should be (and tends to be locally) a very solid IC member/Orlando
> vote deck for the second tournament in a row, it turned out that in both
> this qualifier and the Origins Qualifier, Ben got completely killed in
> two (of 6 total) games by randomly getting his Lutz contested. I pointed
> out that I can't remember the last time that I actually had a vampire
> contested or was in a situation where it was actually problematic that a
> vampire I had in my uncontrolled region was already in play under
> someone else's control (as opposed to it just being mildly annoying),
> and that losing games due to contestation is just incredibly random
> punishment. Yeah, Lutz is really good and really popular, so he is more
> likely to be contested than, like, Gabriel de Cambrai or something, but
> still, having a big important vampire getting contested is both
> incredibly random and usually completely game destroying from very early
> in the game.
>
> As vampire contestation (specifically big vampire contestation--when Old
> Netdecker is contested, it is hardly a problem. When the IC member your
> deck is relying on to go, or whatever, is contested, your game is
> generally over before it even starts) is soooo incredibly random (how
> many vampires are in the game now?), it seems like it might be prudent
> to make it less completely devastating when it happens. What we came up
> with was that maybe the game would work better for all involved if when
> a vampire was contested, instead of both players losing control of that
> vampire, you got to alternate control of him instead. Something like:
>
> "If two (or more) copies of a unique minion are in play, both are
> flipped over and considered out of play. During each player's untap
> phase, they must pay a pool to flip over their copy of the minion into
> play (and flip over their opponent's copy out of play) and may use the
> vampire as normal until their opponent does the same on their untap
> phase. They may choose to not pay a pool and burn their copy of the
> minion immediately."
>
> I'm sure it could be worded better, buy in any case, the end result
> would be that you still burn a pool each turn like normal, but instead
> of just not having a vampire, you get that guy on your turn and until
> your opponent's turn. There certainly could be disparity in terms of how
> long each player has the minion in play, i.e. if me and my prey are
> contesting a guy, I only get the guy on my turn, and then get the guy
> during their turn, and then all the way around the table till my turn
> again, but I suspect that the advantage that was gained by being the
> predator in that situation (i.e. I get my guy to attack my prey and he
> doesn't have that guy to defend himself) would balance that out.

> Well, with the understanding that influence-back rule was added to handle
> contesting issues (and has ended up turning Ecoterrorists and superior Govern
> and the like into bloat tools instead of the pack-building tools they were
> designed to be), I'd say changing something along those lines wouldn't be too

>
> Remove "spend 2 transfers to move 1 counter from a card in your uncontrolled
> region to your pool."
>
> Add "remove from the game a crypt card in your uncontrolled region that would
> contest a card in play to move all blood counters from it to your pool and draw
> a card from your crypt".
>
> And make yielding a crypt card return the crypt card to the permanent
> controller's uncontrolled region, for good measure.

Hm. Those three points are interesting.
I don't like the first one at all. I think it would make slow deck
weaker, because not gaining pool anymore from Powerbase: Montreal or
Ecoterrorists. This would be a major side-effect of a new rule
designed to fix contest issues.

The second point is nice. It fixes the "Oh, blast, my grand prey has
influenced out my 10-cap star" problem. Shouldn't the removal have a
cost (pool or transfers)? Is it intended to allow one to remove for
free all Anarch Converts in crypt (and those drawn this way too) so
all the cards in uncontrolled are non-Anarch Convert minions?

The third point is strange. Sometimes, you want to contest another
player's vampire to weaken him.
Let's have an example:
In the early game, my grand predator has influenced out Anson, and
she's playing an Anson Grooming deck. I am playing an Alexandra /
Anneke / Anson deck. There's no reason for me to kill her, so I don't
influence on Anson. But later on, we're facing each other in duel. Her
strongest card is her Anson. If I manage to shut him down, that'd give
me the upper hand. So I decide to contest Anson.
During her untap phase, she yields the contest. Her copy goes back in
the uncontrolled. And she brings him out anew. So, we are now
contesting 8-cap vampires with 8 blood each. With this new rule (i.e.
"Yielded vampires are returned to the permanent controller's
uncontrolled region"), we are no longer paying for the Contest
(because yielding during the Untap phase, and putting back in play -
well, contested - during the Influence phase). For free when vampire
is at full-cap.

Other example: My prey has her copy of Stavros, with 4 blood left. I
contest Stavros. If my prey wants to get the "free contest" I
discribed just above, it'll cost her 3 pool. But for me, contesting
Stavros is free (just yield in Untap and send back in contest in
Influence). Was that intended?

> and soul gem gives brand new Cybele. No need for voting witch could be
> blocked, don't need to pass trough referendum etc.

Golconda doesn't trigger the Soul Gem (it removes vampires from the
game instead of burning them).

What you want to do is Call the Great Beast to get a new Cybele, then
Villein the new Cybele and the Great Beast and Golconda the Beast so
you can Call him again when you get another skill card.

> About what witness1 wrote
>
> >> This would:
> >> - definitely kill the imbued who just be more like a wallpaper without
> >> pool provided by Travis Traveller
> >That's a really, really dubious assertion.
>
> Ok I played only against one Imbued deck but without TT Imbued have
> lot less poolgain options than vampire based decks, and when Travis
> was out of the game Imbued was near to helpless against most ousting
> decks.

I believe that there are some imbued decks (and, perhaps more
importantly, players) who need Travis in order to survive. Certainly
the imbued would be less good overall if Travis were around. However,
I was top seed in the finals of a recent tournament with a Judgment
deck that had zero copies of Travis because he doesn't have the skill
I was using.

He's not necessary, just good.

-witness1

>

I'm full agree with your proposition
